Industry News: 5 Things Most Developers Get Wrong When Turning Images into HTML

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Turning a design image into a working webpage can look simple.
  • You have a picture (a mockup, a screenshot, a Figma export), and your job is to turn it into working HTML in a browser.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Turning a design image into a working webpage can look simple.

You have a picture (a mockup, a screenshot, a Figma export), and your job is to turn it into working HTML in a browser.

But here is the catch. A design image is static, while a webpage is dynamic and responsive across different screen sizes and devices. A webpage needs to load quickly, adapt perfectly to different screen sizes, and allow touch interactions on mobile devices.

Most mistakes in this process happen when the conversion is treated as copying a picture instead of rebuilding it.

This section walks you through the mistakes developers often make, and more importantly, how to fix each of them.

Whether you are slicing a client mockup or converting a screenshot into code, avoiding these mistakes can save you from hours of rework. Let’s get into the details.

A screenshot reflects how a page appears at a particular display. But it doesn’t show how the layout will behave when the content changes or the screen gets smaller.

Recent findings suggest that developers sometimes try to copy the exact positions and dimensions of every element. To match the screenshot, they may use fixed widths, large margins, and absolute positioning.

This can work at one screen size, but the layout may break on smaller screens or when a heading wraps onto an extra line.

Recent findings suggest that the better approach is identifying the layout rules behind the design. CSS Grid can arrange the cards in columns. Flexbox can help align elements within each card. And media queries can adjust the layout for smaller screens.

Pixel-level comparison can be useful in some cases, but it should not come at the cost of a flexible layout.

It has been revealed that when developers recreate a design, it’s easier for them to focus on shapes and spacing rather than the purpose of each element. So, they may use generic elements for headings, buttons, navigation areas, and content sections instead of choosing elements that reflect each element's purpose.

This may produce the right appearance, but it often makes the code harder to maintain and understand. And when developers fail to use the right HTML elements, it can also create accessibility problems later.

Sources indicate that so don’t put everything inside several unnamed containers. Instead, use a clear structure with appropriate headings, meaningful alt text for informative images, and real buttons for actions.

Semantic elements (e.g., header, nav, main, section, and footer) can also help organize a large page when they match the content’s purpose.

A design image may have headings, descriptions, prices, labels, or button text.

Industry observers note that reusing the entire image to reproduce the original design feels quick. But it can create problems when that text has to work as part of a responsive web page.

For example, there’s a promotional banner that contains a heading, a short description, and a CTA button. If you use the entire banner as one image, you can’t easily change the heading, translate the text, or make the button work as a real element.

It has been revealed that so, don’t treat the image like that. Instead, use the original image where appropriate and recreate the text and button in HTML. CSS can control their position, size, color, and spacing.

Make sure you distinguish between visual elements that should remain images and text that should be recreated as HTML.

Not every part of turning images into HTML needs to be done manually.

Industry observers note that developers sometimes spend too much time on recreating basic elements when there are free online conversion tools available. These tools can help them get an initial version much faster.

An online conversion tool may be helpful when you need to extract text or generate a rough starting layout from a design image.

According to recent reports, for example, you can upload a design image into an online image to html converter to get a starting point (rather than starting from a blank file). Review the tool’s output. Identify the parts you can reuse (as they are) and tweak the parts that need adjustments.

Keep in mind that the first result generated by the tool isn’t the final code. You may need to reorganize the HTML, refine the CSS, and adjust the layout to make it responsive.

Use automation where it saves time and your own judgement where it matters.

A screenshot reveals just one view of a page. It doesn’t show how the layout may change on a phone or how people using a keyboard/screen reader can interact with it.

So, developers who focus only on the desktop design may end up with:.

buttons that are difficult to use.

content that becomes too small on mobile devices.

There’s also a chance of accessibility problems when images lack suitable alt text/interactive elements.

Let’s say a page has three cards in a row. On the desktop, this arrangement may work well. But on a phone, you may need to stack the cards vertically so their content remains readable.

That’s why accessibility should be considered during the same process. Use meaningful headings and provide appropriate alt text for images. Also, maintain sufficient text contrast and make sure interactive elements can be operated with a keyboard.

Lastly, don’t forget to test the page on both desktop and mobile screen sizes before finalizing it.

HTML and CSS handle the structure and appearance of a webpage, but JavaScript makes it possible to add interactive features.

For example, a design image may contain a navigation menu with a button. When recreating this design, developers should make sure the button performs an actual action rather than simply looking like a clickable element.

You can use JavaScript's event listeners to handle these interactions.

Now, add JavaScript to make the menu functional:.

In this example, clicking the button opens or closes the navigation menu. The aria-expanded attribute also communicates the menu's current state to assistive technologies.

Recent findings suggest that this is a simple example of why converting a design image into HTML involves more than matching its appearance. Developers also need to recreate the behavior of interactive elements using appropriate HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

The process of turning an image into HTML feels easy when you treat it the right way.

Recent findings suggest that start by identifying the main sections, text, images, and interactive elements. Then create meaningful HTML and build the layout with CSS. Make the necessary adjustments to ensure it works across different screen sizes.

It has been revealed that use a conversion tool when it can really save time. But don’t forget to review the generated output of the tool thoroughly before using it.

Sources indicate that A screenshot is a visual reference, not a complete set of development instructions. And the best result for you isn’t simply a page that looks like the image.

It is a page that also works well, adapts well, and stays easy to maintain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Corsair's AIR 5400 RS-R midtower PC case is down to its lowest price ever, with a 31% discount bringing the price down to $169.99. The case normally retails for nearly $250, and outside of a short sale last month, we haven't seen it drop below $200. In addition, with a wrap-around glass side panel and triple-chamber design, the case comes with three Corsair RS-R 120mm PWM ARGB fans, which normally run $60 on their own.

Industry observers note that typical of these multi-chamber case designs, the AIR 5400 RS-R supports most hardware you can throw at it. You can use anything from a mini ITX motherboard to an E-ATX board, and it has mounting points for up to two 360mm radiators, plus an additional 120mm mounting point. The 360mm worth of mounting space on the bottom of the case is occupied by the pre-installed fans and an airflow shroud.

In a recent development, additionally, the case is compatible with rear-connector motherboards from Asus, MSI, and Gigabyte, so you can have a cable-free front chamber. The case doesn't have a vertical GPU mount, but there's ample room for even larger graphics cards, with a maximum length of 430 mm supported. Like most multi-chamber cases, this one is primarily designed around liquid cooling. However, you have a generous 180mm of CPU cooler clearance if you decide to go with an air cooler.

The Corsair AIR 5400 RS-R is a midtower PC case with three Corsair RS-R 120mm ARGB fans pre-installed. It supports up to E-ATX motherboards, as well as rear-connector boards from MSI, Asus, and Gigabyte.

The Corsair AIR 1500 RS-R is loaded with enough features to justify its $250 list price, let alone its current sale price of $170. In addition to wide cooling and GPU compatibility, along with rear-connector motherboard support, the case comes with a built-in anti-sag arm to support your GPU, the height of which you can adjust depending on your GPU. Be warned, however, that the final fan on especially long GPUs may hit the support. Thankfully, you can remove it.

Industry observers note that corsair includes its RapidRoute 2.0 mounting system, giving you a pegboard-style motherboard tray that provides mounting points virtually anywhere for cable management. Cable managing multi-chamber cases is much easier than a traditional tower, as well, with ample room behind the motherboard tray to hide your cable mess.

Around the front, the curved-glass side panel indicates off the internals of your rig from the side and front. To get inside, the curved panel splits apart like French doors, so you can service your machine without juggling a few different pieces of tempered glass. The rear side panel is on a hinge for easy access, as well.

The one major downside with this chassis is that it doesn't come with any front panel USB-A ports. Instead, you get three USB-C ports, split between two USB 3.2 Gen 1 ports and a single Gen 2 port, alongside a 3.5mm headphone/microphone combo jack. Given that most motherboards have one or maybe two USB-C ports, extra front panel connectors are always nice to have. However, even a single USB-A would go a long way.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after quickly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked.
  • Industry observers note that the MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player.
  • Industry observers note that while the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after quickly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked. And, after using them, I can see why they sold out so quickly.

Industry observers note that the MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player. The retro style still looks great in 2026, but using an original pair is a bit of a headache in today’s age of headphone jack-less smartphones. So it was nice to see Sony give this a revival with USB-C.

And, yeah, they live up to the hype.

Industry observers note that while the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly. The sound quality is excellent and having a pair of headphones that doesn’t fully enclose my ears is pretty refreshing. There’s no noise cancellation, but with open-ear earbuds becoming more popular, I actually really like these as a similar solution (though high volumes will definitely be heard by those around you). I’m not fully cut off from the world around me, but I’m also able to get good sound quality. Lows are the weakness here, with unimpressive bass drops, but the sound quality is crisp and clear and pretty neutral, and the open-ish style makes it feel like the room around me is filled with music.

It has been revealed that the physical hardware is great. While a plastic and metal build is objectively not as comfy as a premium pair of ANC headphones, the extremely light weight helps MDR-3R become an afterthought. You simply forget you’re wearing them after a few minutes.

The earpads are swappable, with orange and blue options included in the box.

Recent findings suggest that as for the USB-C cable, it’s fully plug-and-play. No app needed and it worked across every device I tested (including Pixel, which doesn’t work with all USB-C audio output). I do wish the cable was perhaps a few inches longer, but it’s long enough to wear the headphones with my phone in my front pocket. There’s a remote along the cable for play/pause and volume adjustments, though I think it’s a little too high on the cable.

For $59.99, these are a fun pair of USB-C headphones to have on hand. They sound good, work great, and don’t cost an arm and a leg. I can see why they sold out so quickly on launch day – in just 10 hours, Sony told me.

Recent findings suggest that sony MDR-3R are back in stock now and shipping in early December. If you want a pair, I say don’t wait. They’re well worth at least trying if you can get them for retail price – please don’t give in to the scalpers selling these at double, they’re not worth that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clicks is still on track to release the phone with a physical keyboard within the next few months, but a Communicator launch before the end of this year isn’t looking very likely as shipping gets pushed back.

The Communicator is a fresh take on what an Android phone can be. It was first introduced at CES earlier this year, with the main selling angle being the physically integrated keyboard. Clicks wants to target those who are looking for a second device, and the Communicator fits the bill.

Industry observers note that last we heard, the Clicks Communicator was on track to launch and ship in December, following a cheery update detailing an upgrade to 12GB of RAM and other changes. However, Clicks posted a new update today stating that the timeline has shifted out a month because of supply chain concerns caused by something other than RAM.

Unfortunately, we’ve encountered a delay with securing a critical supply chain component needed to fabricate our printed circuit board ahead of manufacturing and final assembly. Assembly will now begin in early January, with deliveries expected to start in late January.

It notes that the “critical supply chain component” is the essential fabric used for the tech giant’s printed circuit boards. The blog post dives into some neat details about the component holding things up. The PCBs Clicks is using are made up of more material layers than some competitor boards. But the fabric used to layer those boards is in short supply at this sort of demand, with four manufacturers reportedly unable to meet the company’s required volume.

The post also spells out difficulties caused by troubles in the Middle East, and rising memory costs straining the chain of supply further, even if memory – surprisingly – isn’t the cause of this small delay. Those compounded problems have pushed production back, and people are now told to expect their Clicks Communicator pre-orders to be shipped in late January, at the earliest. Many pre-orders will likely be shipped after that because of further time constraints before Chinese Fresh Year.

In an act of good faith, Clicks notes it’s including a set of 3.5mm wired headphones in each box for orders placed prior to today.

Industry observers note that A push from December to January isn’t massive, and Clicks still seems to be making solid time on developing a form factor we don’t often see. You can still pre-order the Clicks Communicator starting at $649.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that intel's popular Core i7-14700K remains one of the best CPUs for gaming, and it's presently on sale for its lowest price ever at $249.99. The Raptor Lake Refresh CPU ranks well in our CPU benchmark hierarchy, despite being a last-gen chip, and it slots into LGA 1700 motherboards, which are available in both DDR5 and DDR4 varieties. Critically, the Core i7-14700K offers 97% of the gaming performance of the more expensive Core i9-14900K, which is currently selling for $150 more.

When Black Friday sales first spun up, we saw the Core i7-14700K drop to $249.99 at Amazon, and that deal sold out in less than 24 hours. Newegg has the chip available for $299.99, but B&H is at the moment matching the Amazon price. The sale likely won't last long (especially after publishing this article), so you'll want to act fast to get the chip at this price. B&H itself warns that there's "limited supply at this price.".

According to recent reports, the CPU doesn't include a boxed cooler, so you'll need to bring your own. It's unlocked for overclocking, however, given that you slot it into a Z-series motherboard.

As part of the sale, Intel has thrown in its holiday gaming bundle, which allows you to choose two free games out of the following titles: Total War Warhammer 40K, Star Wars Galactic Racer, Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, Lego Batman Legacy of the Dark Knight, Everwind, Battlefield 6, or Assassin's Creed Shadows.

Get 20 total cores, eight performance, and 12 efficiency, with 28 threads and Intel UHD Graphics 770 included.

The Core i7-14700K has become a particularly popular CPU in the past several months, mainly due to DDR5 shortages. Earlier in the year, Intel told us that Raptor Lake remained a critical part of Intel's portfolio, and that it would be that way for "years to come." Now, we're finally seeing the result of promised pricing and inventory adjustments, with the Core i7-14700K dropping to its lowest price ever.

Sources indicate that as you can see from the charts above, the Core i7-14700K remains a potent CPU in both gaming and productivity applications, falling short in the former mainly to AMD's X3D chips. Even in the face of latest Arrow Lake Refresh offerings, 14th-gen CPUs offer competitive performance, and sometimes at a lower price. You get additional upside, too, with support for DDR4 and DDR5 motherboards.

In a recent development, we explored the performance delta between DDR4 and DDR5 on Intel's 14th-gen CPUs, and with the Core i7-14700K, we saw an average drop of 13% in games at 1080p following our normal CPU test suite. That's a significant performance loss, but the Core i7-14700K still manages to match the gaming performance of the Ryzen 7 5800X3D, which is otherwise the fastest DDR4 gaming CPU on the market.

In a recent development, the Core i7-14700K slots into existing LGA 1700 motherboards, though you'll need a Z-series chipset if you want to manually overclock the chip. Although Intel has moved on from the LGA 1700 socket, reports suggest the organization is working on latest 'Raptor Lake Next' chips that will use the same socket.

#92719. A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (309 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Googleblog ↗ Open Full Page

A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (309 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • User interactions with agents today are where computers were in the terminal era: capable, and answering almost everything in text.
  • Sources indicate that today, we're releasing A2UI 1.0, the first stable version of our open protocol for generative UI.
  • With A2UI, the agent describes what to show, and every app draws the UI with its own native components.

User interactions with agents today are where computers were in the terminal era: capable, and answering almost everything in text. Users can ask an agent for anything by typing or talking, and what comes back is usually a wall of text, a poor way to compare three products or edit and approve a detailed plan.

Sources indicate that today, we're releasing A2UI 1.0, the first stable version of our open protocol for generative UI. It lets AI agents answer with interactive screens, such as a form to confirm or a chart. Developers can use it now with open-source renderer SDKs for the web, Android, and iOS and agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. Companies such as Atlassian, Alation, Bloomberg, and ByteDance are already building with it.

With A2UI, the agent describes what to show, and every app draws the UI with its own native components. The application receives A2UI messages and each app renders the content securely and at native speed. Consumers get the same low latency, high trust, and complete native fidelity whether they reach a company's agent in its own app or in a third-party AI assistant that hosts MCP apps, such as Gemini or Claude.

You wake up sick. Getting through the morning takes six apps: book a video visit, move your meetings, tell your team, turn on an out-of-office reply, ask your partner to do school pickup and order soup. Ask a text-only agent instead, and you get a numbered wall of text, then round after round of “which ones?”. A2UI won't handle your sick day, but it gives developers the framework to build an agent that can. That agent could answer with one view of all six apps. Changing your initiative is a couple of taps instead of another round of messages, and nothing is sent until you confirm.

Industry observers note that every e-commerce grid, product page and checkout screen is a shelf. Merchandisers have spent decades working out what to put at eye level, how many choices to show and how to tell whether a display works, and web teams are now rebuilding the same logic in code: sort orders, pinned products, badges, filters and A/B tests. Knowing where those ideas came from helps you build them with fewer mistakes.

According to recent reports, this article maps physical retail merchandising onto digital product design. It covers visual hierarchy and choice load in listing UIs, a small rule-based ranking function you can test, accessible price and badge design with a contrast checker, and a significance test for layout experiments. It also covers why good looks fail at the handoff between design, engineering and operations. The numbers in the examples are illustrative, so use your own data. The code was run with Node.js 22.

Merchandising shapes how products are displayed, promoted and made accessible across sales channels. A well-planned strategy considers visual hierarchy, packaging, promotional materials, inventory timing and consistency between locations. For example, a skincare product may struggle to convert if testers are missing, shelf information is unclear or displays arrive after a campaign begins. If you build for the web, nearly every one of these problems has a direct counterpart:.

Customers scan before they read. Nielsen Norman Group defines visual hierarchy as the arrangement of elements so the eye moves through them in order of importance, and names color and contrast, scale and grouping as the main tools. On a shelf, a larger facing or a contrasting background makes the hero product visible first. In a product grid, the equivalents are a larger card for a featured item, a clear boundary around a bundle, and a restrained use of badges so that only one or two items carry emphasis.

It has been revealed that A common mistake is giving every card a badge, a color and a call to action. When everything is emphasized, nothing is, and the page reads like a crowded table in a store. Treat emphasis as a limited resource and have the design system say how many emphasized cards one screen may show.

A premium item placed beside entry-level alternatives may lose perceived value, and a crowded display can make fresh products look less appealing. Hick’s Law states that the time to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices, and its practical advice is to reduce options when speed matters and to highlight recommended ones. In a listing UI that suggests a curated first screen with a clear sort label, a few high-confidence recommendations and filters that handle the long tail, rather than an unbroken wall of products. Hick’s Law is a guide, not a rule, so treat it as a hypothesis to test on your own audience.

It has been revealed that merchandisers often ask for things like “pin the fresh range to the top, boost this collection, never show more than two items from one brand in a row, and push sold-out items down”. Implemented as scattered CSS order values and one-off queries, these requests become hard to audit. A small, pure function keeps the rules explicit and testable.

Because the function has no side effects, a short test can check every rule. This one confirms that pinned items lead, a pinned item that is out of stock is skipped, the brand cap pushes a third item from one brand behind other brands, sold-out items go last and a boost can lift a weaker product:.

Sources indicate that the design decision here is that stock demotion and the brand cap are defaults, while pins and boosts are inputs a merchandiser can change without a deploy, for example from a config file or admin screen. A real system would also log which rule moved each item, so that someone can answer why a product appears where it does.

According to recent reports, price cards and shelf labels are text, and text needs contrast. The WCAG contrast requirement asks for at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Product cards are a place where this slips, because grey secondary prices and pastel sale badges look refined in a mockup. The following script computes the WCAG contrast ratio, so you can run it over your design tokens in CI.

Sources indicate that it prints 4.54 for mid grey #767676 on white, which just passes for normal text, 7.00 for #595959, which would also meet the stricter enhanced level, and 3.96 for the pink #d94f70, which fails for small badge text but would pass for large text. A sale badge that fails the check should be fixed in the token, not on one page.

A useful display respects the realities of the sales environment: floor space, customer movement, staff workload, replenishment access and how much information shoppers can absorb at a glance. The digital version is the gap between the design file and what ships. Test the setup with the people who will use it, not only with the team that created it, because their feedback reveals practical problems before a wide rollout.

According to recent reports, A polished strategy can fail in practice when materials arrive late, displays are assembled incorrectly or teams miss replenishment. On the web, the matching failures are a promotion that goes live before its product data is synced, a badge that stays on after a sale ends, and a hero banner that links to a discontinued item. Execution needs coordination across marketing, suppliers, logistics and engineering, with clear instructions, realistic schedules, display standards and checks. Some companies outsource this kind of field merchandising. One provider’s services page, for example, lists planogram and retail resets, end-cap displays, signage placement, on-shelf availability, in-store audits and visit reporting. Whether or not you hire help, that list is a useful checklist of what execution involves, and most items have a digital twin you can automate: availability checks, expiry dates on promotions and audit reports. Treat any performance figures on vendor pages as the vendor’s own claims and ask for evidence before relying on them.

In a recent development, timing matters most for seasonal promotions and limited windows. A campaign that goes live after peak demand has passed cannot deliver the same value, so give promotional content a start and end date in the data model and have a scheduled job remove it, rather than relying on someone to remember.

In a recent development, sales alone cannot tell you whether visibility, placement, stockouts, confusing information or poor setup caused a result. For a web listing, the answer is a controlled experiment. The script below compares conversion for a control grid and a variant with a two-proportion z-test, a standard way to check whether a difference is larger than chance would explain.

According to recent reports, with these illustrative numbers, conversion rises from 3.00 percent to 3.90 percent, a relative lift of 30.0 percent, and the z value of 2.21 exceeds the 1.96 threshold for roughly 95 percent confidence. That does not prove the curated grid is better in general. It says this difference is unlikely to be noise for this test, and it assumes you fixed the sample size in advance and did not stop the moment the result looked good. Use a proper experimentation platform or a statistician for anything with real revenue at stake.

A strong merchandising operation does not require a large budget. A simple guide for product priorities, layout, pricing, replenishment and approved materials keeps execution consistent, and it is the physical version of a design system: a small set of approved components and rules that make the correct result the easy path. For a product card, that means a documented component with a fixed set of badge types, a defined maximum of emphasized items per screen and tokens that already pass the contrast check.

Sources indicate that consistency also protects trust. Damaged fixtures, inconsistent packaging, missing prices and outdated signs make good products look poorly managed, and the digital equivalents are broken images, stale prices and mismatched labels between the listing and the product page. Aim for consistency, not identical pages: a mobile grid and a kiosk screen can differ, but they should share product priorities, visual identity and core messages.

Sources indicate that temporary and in-store selling spaces demand quick communication. Visitors move fast, attention is limited, and interfaces must be clear from a distance and forgiving of mistakes. If you build kiosk, tablet or point-of-sale software, these constraints shape the interface:.

Recent findings suggest that when results disappoint, audit the real experience before commissioning a redesign. Think like a first-time customer: is the offer clear, are premium items distinct and can the team maintain the page easily? Government small-business guidance offers concrete analogues. The Queensland Government’s retail display guidance recommends showing essential information and prices so customers can decide quickly, placing popular or profitable items at eye level, and refreshing window displays every two to four weeks. The Westminster City Council guide similarly links visual merchandising, layout and planned promotions to attracting customers and encouraging them to spend more time and money in a business.

Prioritize visibility, clarity, stock accuracy and consistent execution before investing in a full redesign. Small operational improvements can make a meaningful difference, especially when they remove obstacles that repeatedly interrupt the buying process.

Sources indicate that the public guidance cited here was written for general small-business use, and UX principles such as visual hierarchy and Hick’s Law come from interface research, so they are useful analogies rather than guarantees. The code is a teaching sketch: it ignores personalization, pagination, caching, search relevance and many other concerns of a production ranking system. Results vary with category, audience and device, so test changes in your own setting and treat any benchmark as a starting point.

What is merchandising in e-commerce? It is how products are displayed, ordered, promoted and made accessible across a site or app, including layout, labels, badges, sort rules and inventory handling.

According to recent reports, how does visual hierarchy apply to a product grid? The same tools apply: contrast, scale and grouping decide what the eye sees first and which products read as related.

Recent findings suggest that what should I measure first? Start with conversion, add-to-cart rate and stock availability for the listing, then add average order value and revenue per visitor once the basics are tracked.

How do I know a layout test is reliable? Fix the sample size in advance, randomize users, run it long enough to cover weekly patterns and check significance, for example with the two-proportion test above.

Do small teams need a major design system? No. A short component guide with a few badge types, spacing rules and accessible color tokens is enough to keep pages consistent.

Merchandising is applied interface design with a long history. Clear hierarchy, a curated first screen, readable prices, explicit ranking rules and controlled experiments carry over directly from the shelf to the screen. For designers and developers, the practical lesson is that a good layout only counts if it ships correctly, stays current and is measured. Audit the basics, put the rules in code, test one change at a time and record what you learn.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yes, the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra remains a good buy in late 2026 if you want a large-screen Android phone with versatile cameras, an integrated S Pen, and long-term software support.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra has aged very well, benefiting from Samsung’s mature hardware and software, along with a host of other quality-of-life improvements gained from its recent enhancement to One UI 9 running Android 17.

We’re going to take a deeper dive at what the S26 Ultra is, and how it compares to its cheaper siblings, in a quest to figure out whether it’s still worth your time and money this holiday season.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra is the highest-end model in Samsung’s 2026 Galaxy S26 lineup. Released back on March 11, it pairs a 6.9-inch display with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor, a built-in S Pen, and a four-camera system led by a 200MP main sensor.

It has been revealed that it’s a powerful device, built for photography enthusiasts and professionals who want to get the most out of their phones while on the go. Its large screen size belies a relatively compact, portable device that’s a pleasure to do work on, from writing emails to taking photos to taking meeting notes using the S Pen.

According to recent reports, its most distinctive feature is Privacy Display. Rather than relying on an awkward screen protector, the Galaxy S26 Ultra can reduce off-angle visibility when needed. You can apply protection to selected apps or sensitive notifications instead of obscuring everything all the time. That’s useful when checking messages on a train or opening personal information in a busy restaurant.

In our Galaxy S26 Ultra review, we talked about how the Privacy Display is flexible and useful, able to be enabled for certain apps and left off for others.

In a recent development, we also found dependable everyday endurance from the 5,000mAh battery, and now that the phone supports 60-watt wired charging, quick top-ups become more useful. Samsung also promises seven generations of OS upgrades and seven years of security updates from launch, an important consideration if you proposal to keep your next phone for several years.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s main advantages over the Galaxy S26 and S26+ are Privacy Display, the integrated S Pen, and its more versatile camera hardware.

Recent findings suggest that at launch, US pricing started at $899.99 for the Galaxy S26, $1,099.99 for the Galaxy S26+, and $1,299.99 for the Galaxy S26 Ultra, each with 256GB of storage. But those prices have dropped over the past few months, and you may be able to get them for less. We’ve seen the S26 Ultra, for example, as low as $999.99 during Prime Day.

Here are the specs for each model:.

As our Galaxy S26 launch coverage detailed, Privacy Display is exclusive to the Ultra. Its camera system also adds flexibility through separate 3x and 5x telephoto cameras, alongside the 200MP main camera and 50MP ultrawide.

Having different lenses gives you more options for portraits, travel photos, and subjects you can’t easily walk closer to.

The regular Galaxy S26 is the more natural choice if you prioritize a smaller phone and a lower purchase price. The Galaxy S26+ makes sense if you want a large-screen Galaxy without paying for Ultra-specific features.

The biggest improvement since launch is the move from Android 16-based One UI 8.5 to Android 17-based One UI 9.

One UI 9 offers several practical additions. Now Nudge suggestions extend beyond the keyboard into conversation notifications and a floating button. The quick panel offers more customization, and Samsung DeX gains easier movement between desktops and desktop previews in Recents.

Samsung has also made Smart Switch even better, which allows you to swiftly and easily port over your apps, data, and media from another device.

Industry observers note that the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s features are most useful when they solve problems or make everyday moments feel joyful and seamless. Here are five examples:.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra is still Samsung’s best non-foldable phone, and one of the best phones you can buy right now, period. From its awesome cameras to its peerless S Pen to its unique Privacy Display, it has something for everyone.

If you’re coming from a Galaxy S22 or S23 series phone, there are so many upgrades, small and large, that are awaiting you with the S26 Ultra.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra and Samsung’s other products are on sale during Best Buy’s Holiday Deals event.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Fitbit Air is one of my favorite products of 2026 and my preferred workout companion, but not being able to see a workout while you’re in the middle of it has been a huge complaint of mine, and the latest Google Health enhancement is fixing that.

Quite literally at the start of this week, I was on a walk through my neighborhood and though to myself, “it’s still pretty annoying that I can’t see my workout progress in the Google Health app.” It’s been a complaint of mine for a while, as various treadmill sessions and more have left me wondering what my heart rate is looking like, how many steps I’ve taken, etc, and it’s only a problem when using the Fitbit Air, seeing as the Pixel Watch (or Fitbit Edge) I’d wear otherwise will show that data front and center.

Google Health 5.13 is fixing that.

In a recent development, in the changelog for Google Health 5.13, Google details a new “exercise in-progress” card on the main “Today” screen. This will show what exercise is being tracked and also let you end the workout early.

If you use your Pixel Watch, Fitbit Air, or Fitbit Edge to automatically track your exercises, you’ll now see an exercise-in-progress card on your mobile app’s Today screen. This card lets you know that your device is tracking your exercise and gives you the opportunity to end the tracking and get your summary whenever you want.

We don’t know exactly what this card looks like just yet, but it sounds like it fits the need perfectly.

Google Health 5.13 is now rolling out on Android and iOS.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming leak suggests that Samsung is preparing to copy the iPhone’s Dynamic Island feature in the not-too-distant future, to an extent that not many other Android brands have even done thus far.

Copying the Dynamic Island was briefly like a rite of passage for some Android brands, with many wasting almost no time in delivering their own version of the feature. But, on many of those devices, it’s a surface-level ripoff at best. The feature is primarily limited to music apps and timers, rarely working with any third-party apps in meaningful ways. Android has a built-in feature similar to Apple’s but not in the same styling.

Samsung is now preparing its own version of the Dynamic Island, and it seems this one has a bit more meat on its bones.

Recent findings suggest that samMobile on Twitter/X posted a video and two still images of what appears to be a Dynamic Island clone coming to Galaxy devices. It’s mentioned as potentially coming to the Galaxy S27 series (so, One UI 9.5) and being called “Moment Effects.” A portion of the software explicitly mentions integration with Google Sports, the leak claims, while it seems Samsung is using Live Notifications here, which already support a number of third-party apps.

The kicker from a UX perspective is that Samsung’s interpretation allows you to swipe between activities, similar to Apple, but the core premise is similar with the island showing around the selfie camera cutout.

Industry observers note that when this feature might surface does remain unclear, but a One UI 9.5 debut would make plenty of sense. That enhancement is in beta now and due to launch on the Galaxy S27 series early next year.

Recent findings suggest that what do you think of Samsung’s alleged Dynamic Island clone? Personally, I’m on board as long as it proves useful, and it seems to be on the right track compared to most other copycats.

Folding phones have come in numerous variations over the years as the concept has evolved. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the latest evolution that introduces a form factor that fits every user. Its unique design makes it a foldable most people can actually use – which makes it a perfect gift. You might be surprised by what it can do.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

Industry observers note that it’s in the name. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 folds and unfolds like other foldable devices – that much you know. But what the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s form factor provides is something different to what most might be familiar with.

According to recent reports, instead of a tall device that unfolds into a near-uniform square display, you get a wider screen more like a tablet. That makes it perfect for watching videos or movies. Content that naturally works well on TVs or your computer will look great on the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

In a recent development, what about content that’s best viewed in portrait mode? Because it opens up to a tablet-like display, you can turn the Fold 8 to watch YouTube Shorts or Instagram Reels without a problem, so if you or someone you know likes to watch content on a bigger display, the Z Fold 8 makes that much easier. It really doesn’t matter what content you come across – the wider inner display gives you that large screen feeling.

Like a well-designed tool, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has more purposes than the tasks best suited for the inner display. That shorter, wider profile makes the outer display smaller, but not as thin as something on other foldables, like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

In reality, the aspect ratio is similar enough across both the inner and outer screens that most content scales well on the shorter front panel. Social apps like X and Instagram look great because videos and images are able to fill the screen, rather than squeeze. Samsung’s One UI software also supports app optimization across both screens, although the experience may vary by app.

Saying the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s outer display is “minimal” isn’t a dig, either. Apps can be refreshing to use when you don’t need to open them on a large scale. Take Messages, for instance. It’s not a complex app, and there isn’t a ton to see – just the last couple of messages exchanged. The same goes for plenty of apps available on the Google Play Store.

And guess what? If you don’t like using the app on a smaller display, just unfold the phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is such a versatile phone, whether it’s a gift during the holidays or one for yourself.

There are instances where you need the large real estate. One UI 9 gives the Galaxy Z Fold 8 the option to open and run multiple apps on your screen. There are several ways you can do it, too.

The main approach is to split two apps on the wide inner display. But if you want to see more from one app, you can simply drag the split over in one direction. One UI 9 leaves room to add one more app to that split screen, giving you a three-way Split View. All it takes is dragging an app from the taskbar and choosing the spot.

If you truly need a fourth app open, you have the option to open another in a floating window. Having four apps open at once is definitely a niche instance, but the Galaxy Z Fold 8 handles it like it’s nothing. You can have YouTube up in one corner while you check Messages for gift ideas and shop through the Amazon app. It might be helpful to keep a list of what you got and for whom in a floating Sheets window.

According to recent reports, the point is not only that it’s technically possible, but it’s usable. So often devices let users open apps in split screen, but are in no way comfortable enough for the task. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is perfect for it, and the experience actually makes you more productive, not less.

Most phones don’t let you get the best angle without any sort of third-party accessory. The Galaxy Z Fold 8, though, acts like its own tripod in a way.

Recent findings suggest that let’s say you’re taking photos, and you need to get a shot of yourself, but no one is around to take the photo for you. The Galaxy Z Fold 8’s hinge lets it prop itself up, so you can do things like set a timer and run to strike a pose.

This comes in handy for videos, too. Think of how many times you wanted to get a good angle on a plane or somewhere where there’s this flat surface just asking for a tiny tripod or kickstand. Well, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is its own kickstand and can be positioned at just the right angle.

Google has thoroughly redesigned Gemini for Android’s in-app camera that lets you rapidly add an image to prompts.

Available from the ‘plus’ menu in the prompt box, the old interface launched a fullscreen viewfinder that was quite generic. This UI is still in use when you launch the camera from the Gemini overlay.

Recent findings suggest that the fresh one appears inline on the Gemini homepage or inside a conversation. It releases as a bottom sheet that you can drag up — with a really slick animation — to take up most of the screen.

This nearly edge-to-edge redesign, which extends behind the system navigation bar, is a stark contrast to the old approach.

To the right of the capture button is a three-dot overflow button that animates on open, revealing options to control the flash and switch to the front-facing camera. There’s a back button on the other side, but you can also just swipe down.

This camera redesign first debuted in the Gemini for iOS app, but has now widely rolled out on Android in both the beta and stable (version 17.76+) channels. Be sure to Force stop the Google app if you’re not seeing it live yet.

This follows the launch of GIF creation in the Gemini app yesterday. Powered by Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, select GIF from the Format menu or specify “Create a GIF” in your prompt. Google frames this feature as an alternative to searching for GIFs.

Say hello to GIFs in Gemini. Say goodbye to searching for the perfect one.From looping photo effects to funny memes, create any GIF you can imagine with our latest video model, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, for smooth motion and consistent quality across every frame.

#92693. Sizing GPU Memory for a RAG Service: KV Cache, Context and Concurrency

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1116 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sitepoint ↗ Open Full Page

Sizing GPU Memory for a RAG Service: KV Cache, Context and Concurrency

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app is usually drawn as a language model plus a vector database.
  • This article indicates how to estimate that limit before you deploy, with a short script you can run, and then covers what else in the pipeline can slow responses down.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app is usually drawn as a language model plus a vector database. When it goes live, the part that fails first is rarely the retrieval. It is GPU memory on the generation model, because a model that loads fine for one request can run out of memory when several users send long questions at once.

This article indicates how to estimate that limit before you deploy, with a short script you can run, and then covers what else in the pipeline can slow responses down.

In a recent development, serving a model takes more than its weights. The GPU also holds:.

the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with the length of every active request.

activations and batching overhead.

memory used by the inference runtime itself.

SitePoint's guide to running a local LLM on 10GB of VRAM makes the same point for a single desktop GPU: the usable budget is the total VRAM minus overhead, and the KV cache grows with the context window, so the real model budget is smaller than the number on the box.

For a RAG service, the KV cache matters even more. Retrieved passages are pasted into the prompt, so every request carries a long context, and every concurrent request holds its own cache.

The cache size per token depends on the model's architecture: two tensors (keys and values) for every layer, for every KV head. This script turns those numbers into a rough limit on concurrent requests:.

def kv_bytes_per_token(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes=2):.

# Keys and values, for every layer, for one token.

return 2 *layers *kv_heads *head_dim *dtype_bytes.

def max_concurrent(vram_gb, weights_gb, ctx_tokens, per_token, reserve_gb=2.0):.

budget = (vram_gb - weights_gb - reserve_gb) * GIB.

return int(budget // (ctx_tokens * per_token)).

per_token = kv_bytes_per_token(32, 8, 128).

print(per_token // 1024, "KiB per token").

for ctx in (4096, 8192, 16384):.

n = max_concurrent(24, 16, ctx, per_token).

print(ctx, "tokens ->", n, "concurrent requests").

For a 24 GB GPU holding about 16 GB of fp16 weights with 2 GB kept in reserve, it prints:.

4096 tokens -> 12 concurrent requests.

8192 tokens -> 6 concurrent requests.

16384 tokens -> 3 concurrent requests.

Recent findings suggest that the numbers are estimates. Real runtimes add their own overhead, and the architecture values come from the model's configuration file, so read them from the model you actually use. The pattern is what matters: doubling the context length halves the number of requests that fit. A RAG prompt that stuffs in ten retrieved chunks costs real capacity.

Serving runtimes do not simply crash when the cache is full. The vLLM documentation on optimization and tuning explains that when KV cache space is insufficient for all batched requests, the engine preempts some of them and recomputes them later, which can hurt end-to-end latency. Its suggested remedies include giving the cache more memory, reducing the number of concurrent sequences or batched tokens, or sharding the model across GPUs.

In a recent development, so the symptom of undersizing is often not an error. It is slow, uneven responses under load. Test with realistic prompt lengths and several simultaneous people, not a single request.

It has been revealed that embedding and ingestion have a different profile from generation. Embedding is often lighter than serving a large language model, and some teams run it on CPU. Document parsing, chunking and tokenization also run on CPU, so a fast GPU cannot make up for a slow CPU upstream. SitePoint's tutorial on a local RAG system for private documents walks through chunking, embeddings, vector storage and reranking, and is a good map of which stages run where.

RAM: vector indexes, document loaders and caches all live in system memory, so large collections need more of it.

Storage: model files, indexes, logs and backups add up. Fast storage shortens model loading and re-indexing.

Network: if the vector database, application server and model server sit in different places, latency adds to every request.

Two layouts are common. A single instance runs everything and is simplest for prototypes and internal tools. Separated services put ingestion and retrieval on smaller machines and keep the GPU for generation, which scales better as traffic grows.

Memory estimates only hold if the GPU memory is really yours. On a shared or time-sliced GPU, other workloads can take memory and compute away from your service, which makes capacity hard to proposal. Hosting providers describe this in different terms, such as passthrough, vGPU, MIG and time-slicing. For a view of how one GPU hosting provider explains those allocation methods, GPU Mart's GPU virtualization guide compares them. It is a hosting organization's page, so confirm any provider's claims about isolation and performance with your own load test.

Whatever provider you choose, ask these questions:.

Is the physical GPU assigned to you exclusively, or partitioned or time-sliced?

Do you have root access to install your own drivers, CUDA libraries and containers?

Which minimum commitments, regions and support terms apply?

A small stack can run as a handful of containers: an API service for request handling and prompt assembly, an ingestion worker, a vector database and a model server. Keeping them separate lets you monitor each one's memory and CPU use and move the heavy one to bigger hardware without rewriting the rest.

Sources indicate that for a service that stays up all month, a fixed monthly term is easier to forecast than hourly capacity. Hourly capacity suits testing quantization settings or processing a one-off document batch.

Is GPU memory always the bottleneck for RAG?

Industry observers note that not always. Generation usually hits memory first, but slow parsing, a small CPU or a distant vector database can dominate response time.

Does quantization solve the memory problem?

It has been revealed that it shrinks the weights, but the KV cache still grows with context length and concurrency. Test with your real prompt sizes.

Should embeddings run on the GPU?

It depends on volume. Small workloads can run on CPU, while a large ingestion job may benefit from a GPU for a limited time.

Size a RAG service for the worst realistic moment, not the single-request demo. Estimate the KV cache from the model's architecture, remember that long retrieved contexts reduce how many requests fit, watch for preemption under load, keep CPU, RAM, storage and network in the blueprint, and find out whether the GPU is exclusive or shared. The script above is small, but it turns a vague worry about memory into numbers you can check.

A federal judge has barred Illinois from licensing, taxing or prosecuting sports event contracts listed on CFTC-regulated exchanges. The state's appeal sends the fight to the Seventh Circuit, which already has prediction-market cases from Wisconsin.

According to recent reports, illinois has lost, for now, its power to police sports event contracts traded on federally regulated exchanges. Judge Martha Pacold’s order in the Northern District of Illinois turns her early-October ruling into a formal injunction. It covers contracts listed on CFTC-regulated platforms such as Kalshi and Coinbase.

The order reaches three state tools. They are the Sports Wagering Act, the criminal gambling statute and an Illinois Gaming Board internet-wagering rule. The budget’s prediction-market fees fall with the licensing rules, because they apply only to providers holding a state license. Her first ruling had left the tax question open and called for more argument on the fees.

The stakes are significant. Fiscal 2026 was the first year of the state’s per-wager tax on licensed sports wagering.

Sources indicate that the Gaming Board had already tried to act. It sent cease-and-desist letters to KalshiEX, Crypto.com and Robinhood on April 1, 2025. Polymarket received one on Jan. 27, 2026. Those letters cited the Sports Wagering Act (230 ILCS 45) and the criminal code (720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)).

Recent findings suggest that lawmakers then took a different route. Gov. JB Pritzker signed the budget containing the new framework on June 16. Under the package, which includes SB 3019, prediction markets became exchange wagers under the Sports Wagering Act and needed a Gaming Board license. Each transaction carried a tax that would climb once a licensee passed five million exchange wagers. In September, Republican Rep. Travis Weaver filed House Bill 5811 to repeal the exchange-wager tax. His bill would leave the licensing rules in place.

It has been revealed that licensed online and mobile sportsbooks face their own costs. A first license for that category costs $15 million and runs four years, with each four-year renewal priced at $1 million.

Sources indicate that courts are divided on whether state gambling laws reach CFTC-regulated sports contracts. Pacold’s order is a rare win for Kalshi and the federal regulator. Before her early-October decision, Kalshi had lost 16 federal court rulings in a row. In that opinion, Pacold found the state’s other laws in conflict with federal law because they control “what can be sold, as well as where it can be sold and to whom.”.

In a recent development, the CFTC sued Arizona, Connecticut and Illinois on April 2, 2026, over their actions against federally registered designated contract markets. Chairman Michael Selig stated the agency would defend market participants against “overzealous state regulators.”.

There are now 5 prediction-market appeals before the Seventh Circuit involving sports-event contracts:.

The outcome now depends on a single appeals court.

Industry observers note that on July 29, Judge William Griesbach ruled against the CFTC in Wisconsin, and the agency took that case to the Chicago-based court. Illinois has asked the Seventh Circuit to reverse and vacate Pacold’s order.

Nebraska voters appear to reject online sports betting despite nearly $22.5 million campaign

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readwrite

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Both linked measures to legalize mobile wagering through Nebraska's racetrack casinos trailed in unofficial returns.
  • Nebraska voters appear to have turned down online sports betting.
  • It has been revealed that A loss would be a rare setback for the industry at the ballot box.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Both linked measures to legalize mobile wagering through Nebraska's racetrack casinos trailed in unofficial returns. A defeat would close off a fresh market for sportsbooks and indicates that doubts about tax relief can beat a heavily funded campaign.

Nebraska voters appear to have turned down online sports betting. Initiatives 440 and 441 would have amended the state constitution and statutes to allow mobile wagering through the state’s licensed racetrack casinos. The Secretary of State’s unofficial count, with 885 of 1,322 precincts fully reporting, had 440 trailing by about 296,000 to 354,000. The companion measure, 441, trailed by about 299,000 to 351,000. The results are not yet certified.

It has been revealed that A loss would be a rare setback for the industry at the ballot box. Betting would stay in-person only at Nebraska’s five racetrack casinos. FanDuel, DraftKings and the racetrack operators would not gain a fresh market. Initiative sponsor Jordan McGrain called the midnight results “pretty clear.”.

Recent findings suggest that tax relief was the core of the pitch. Supporters projected more than $166 million for the state’s property tax credit fund over ten years. Opponents countered that the money would flow to out-of-state gambling companies. Nebraska at the moment taxes casino gaming revenue at 20 percent. Of that tax, 70 percent goes to property tax relief credits.

In a recent development, A report commissioned by Tax Relief Nebraska, the committee behind the measures, estimated just under $87 million in new state tax revenue over five years. That projection did not carry the vote. Joey Spellerberg, the state treasurer, backed the opposition and noted voters saw the promised tax benefits as negligible.

Should the unofficial result stand, gambling-harm arguments and doubts about tax relief would have carried a heavily outspent opposition to victory. That is a warning for future online casino and sports betting pushes in other states. It also comes as lawmakers are already restricting sweepstakes and prediction markets.

Sources indicate that the ballot route followed repeated failures in the Legislature. Lawmakers did not send a similar constitutional amendment to voters, including in 2024 and 2025. Tax Relief Nebraska then submitted more than 201,000 signatures for the amendment in late June 2026. It filed 146,000 for the companion statute. Election officials flagged possibly fraudulent signatures collected during the drive.

Funding also drew scrutiny. FanDuel and MGM subsidiary Roar Digital gave more than $3.5 million combined to Tax Relief Nebraska. The Legal Accountability Center asked the state’s disclosure commission to investigate. It cited the companies’ ownership in Ireland and the UK.

The proposed market was tightly drawn. Each racetrack gaming operator could have offered wagering through at most two online platforms. Wagering servers would have had to be located in Nebraska. State regulators would have had until June 1, 2027, to adopt rules for online wagering.

The count now moves toward certification. County abstracts of votes must reach the Secretary of State by November 23. State canvassers meet on November 30, 2026, at 11:30 a.m. to certify the results. Recounts in eligible races start December 2 at 9 a.m.

Generating a single AI video clip is easy now. You send a prompt and get a few seconds of footage back. The trouble starts when the goal is three, five, or ten minutes of video where the same character looks the same in every scene, the style does not drift, and the captions line up with the picture.

According to recent reports, most guides stop at the clip. This one covers the part after it, treating a video as a small build pipeline: a storyboard that is data, prompts generated from that data, clips normalised and stitched with ffmpeg, and captions derived from the same source. If you want to wire a generation model into your own application first, SitePoint's guide to integrating generative video APIs into web applications covers the request and webhook side. If the finished video is headed to a YouTube channel, how to get a YouTube API key and use the Data API is a good starting point for the publishing side. Everything between those two is below.

Long-form AI video fails at the seams between clips, not inside them. Plan for continuity before you generate anything.

A storyboard stored as JSON can be validated, versioned, diffed, and turned into prompts by code, which a pile of loose prompts cannot.

Recent findings suggest that repeat the full character description in every prompt. Models do not remember the previous clip.

Recent findings suggest that clips from different generations rarely share resolution, frame rate, or codec settings. Normalise them before joining.

Captions are cheapest when generated from the script and measured clip durations, not transcribed afterwards.

Recent findings suggest that current video models generate short clips, commonly a handful of seconds each. A longer video is therefore many clips, and every clip is an independent generation. The model has no memory of what the character wore in the previous one.

Industry observers note that that produces three kinds of failure. The character drifts, so hair, clothing, or proportions change between scenes. The style drifts, so lighting and colour grade shift from cut to cut. And the technical specs drift, so one clip is 24 frames per second at one resolution and the next is something else. Each of these is fixable, but only if the project is organised so the fixes can be applied consistently.

Industry observers note that start with a structured storyboard instead of a document full of prompts. One file holds the style, a "character bible", and an ordered list of scenes.

"project": "rainy-day-lantern",.

"style": "soft watercolor picture book illustration, warm evening light, 16:9",.

"mira": "a nine year old girl with short curly black hair, a yellow raincoat and red rubber boots",.

"lantern": "a small round paper lantern with a gentle orange glow and a tiny smiling face".

"setting": "a narrow cobblestone street in light rain",.

"action": "walks slowly past closed shops, looking up at the sky",.

"camera": "slow push in from a medium shot",.

"narration": "It had rained all afternoon, and the street was quiet.".

"characters": ["mira", "lantern"],.

"setting": "under a bakery awning",.

"action": "finds the lantern glowing on a wooden crate and kneels beside it",.

"camera": "static medium close up",.

"narration": "Then she noticed something glowing under the awning.".

It has been revealed that because it is data, a script can check it before you spend any generation credits. Two checks pay for themselves quickly: every character named in a scene must exist in the bible, and no scene may be longer than the clip limit of the model you use.

Treat MAX_CLIP_SECONDS as a setting. Limits differ between models and change over time, so check the one you are using rather than trusting the number in this example.

Never write the per-scene prompt by hand. Generate it, so the style line and the character descriptions are identical every time.

Changing a detail, say the colour of the boots, becomes one edit in the bible instead of a search through twenty prompts, and the diff shows exactly what changed between versions.

Put the style line first and keep it identical across all scenes.

Industry observers note that describe one action per clip. Two sequential actions in one prompt often produce a blend of both.

Keep camera directions simple. A single move per clip is more reliable than a combination.

According to recent reports, avoid naming real people, brands, or existing characters in prompts. Beyond the rights concern, it makes results harder to reproduce.

Clips from separate generations often disagree on resolution, frame rate, pixel format, or codec parameters. Joining them directly can produce stutters, green frames, or an outright error. Convert every clip to one agreed format first.

-vf "scale=1280:720:force_original_aspect_ratio=decrease,pad=1280:720:(ow-iw)/2:(oh-ih)/2,fps=24,format=yuv420p" \.

-an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 "norm/$(basename "$f")".

The filter scales each clip to fit a 1280 by 720 frame, adds padding if the aspect ratio differs, sets 24 frames per second, and forces a widely compatible pixel format. The -an flag drops any audio the model generated, since narration will be added as one track later. Name clips with zero padded numbers such as s01.mp4 and s02.mp4, so a shell glob sorts them in story order.

Once every file shares the same parameters, the concat demuxer can join them without re-encoding:.

for f in norm/*.mp4; do echo "file '$PWD/$f'"; done > list.txt.

ffmpeg -y -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c copy stitched.mp4.

Sources indicate that hard cuts are the safe default. Crossfades are possible with ffmpeg's xfade filter, but they require careful offset arithmetic and a re-encode, so add them only when a cut genuinely looks wrong.

Industry observers note that captions are easiest when they come from the script, not from a speech recognition pass over the finished video. The storyboard already holds the narration text and each scene's length, so an SRT file is a few lines of code. Use measured durations rather than planned ones, because a generated clip is often a little shorter or longer than requested.

function toTimestamp(totalSeconds) {.

const ms = Math.round(totalSeconds * 1000);.

const h = String(Math.floor(ms / 3600000)).padStart(2, '0');.

Patch each scene's duration from measureSeconds on the normalised clip before calling buildSrt. If a narration line is long, split it across two caption blocks so it stays readable. Then combine picture, voiceover, and captions in one final step:.

ffmpeg -y -i stitched.mp4 -i narration.mp3 -i captions.srt \.

Soft captions like these can be switched off by the viewer and read by assistive technology, which is better than burning text into the picture. Keep the .srt file as well, since most platforms accept it as a separate upload.

Industry observers note that everything above is a good fit when you need repeatability: many videos from templates, versioned storyboards, automated publishing, or tight control over the model. The price is that you own the glue code, the ffmpeg settings, and the failures.

In a recent development, for one off projects, or when the people making the video are not developers, a managed platform is often the more sensible choice. Tools such as magiclight.ai bundle story to video generation, character handling, voice, and an editor in one interface, and advertise videos of up to 50 minutes. Check the specifics yourself, because claims like that are marketing, and results depend on your content. One point matters for developers in particular: if you need to automate generation from your own code, confirm that the platform you pick offers an API or export route before you build a workflow around it. A tool with a good editor and no programmatic access suits a different job than the pipeline in this article.

According to recent reports, A short manual pass catches what automation does not. Watch the whole video once at normal speed, looking only at continuity. Read the captions against the audio. Check that no real person's likeness, brand mark, or protected character slipped into the footage. Finally, check the disclosure rules of the platform you publish on, since many now ask creators to label realistic synthetic media, and the rules change.

The model is only one component of a long-form AI video. The reliability comes from the structure around it: a validated storyboard, prompts generated from it, clips forced into one format, and captions derived from measured data. Each of those is ordinary software engineering, and none of it depends on which generation model you choose, so the pipeline survives when the model changes.

Start with a two minute video and four or five scenes. Fix the seams there before scaling up, because every continuity problem you find at that size is one you will not have to hunt for in a ten minute project.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that voters in Allen, DeKalb and Steuben counties each rejected inland casino gambling by double digits on November 3.
  • Industry observers note that with the measure defeated, the license created by House Enrolled Act 1038 cannot be granted by the Indiana Gaming Commission.
  • Recent findings suggest that allen County, where developers were seeking to build, carried the most weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that voters in Allen, DeKalb and Steuben counties each rejected inland casino gambling by double digits on November 3. The single new license in House Enrolled Act 1038, tied to a project of at least $500 million, now has no county that can host it.

Industry observers note that with the measure defeated, the license created by House Enrolled Act 1038 cannot be granted by the Indiana Gaming Commission. A repeat ballot is also off the table. State law bars a second public question in any county that voted the measure down.

Recent findings suggest that allen County, where developers were seeking to build, carried the most weight. The county’s election-night summary counted 102,935 votes on the question, with 40.44% in favor. In DeKalb County, 7,374 voters said no. Steuben County recorded 6,234 no votes.

The stakes were substantial. That minimum investment had to cover both the casino and its non-gambling amenities. At least 60% of that had to be spent within two years of the award. The license also carried a $150 million fee to the state, with $50 million of it going to a fund for former host communities hurt by casino closures.

The projected public return was large as well. A study done for the Indiana Gaming Commission estimated that an Allen County casino could generate $204 million in revenue alongside its annual state tax payments. Under the act, 10% of the casino’s tax payments would have gone to the northeast Indiana regional development authority.

The process hinged on the vote from the start. The commission’s July guidance said it would take applications only for a county or counties where voters approved inland casino gambling. None did.

Gaming Commission officials said that with no county passing the referendum, nothing happens, and that any next steps are up to the legislature. That puts operators back in front of lawmakers.

Lawmakers have already redrawn this map once. Instead of creating a latest license, a January 22, 2026 committee version of House Bill 1038 would have relocated the Ohio County riverboat license. That inland casino could have gone to Allen, DeKalb, Steuben or Wayne County. The enacted version instead created one new license and eliminated one unused racino license. Indianapolis was kept off the list because a casino there would pull business from the existing casinos in Shelbyville and Anderson.

DeKalb and Steuben counties have turned away a casino in referendum votes. Allen County is still counting but 'no' is leading. https://t.co/rwMo6sIYZ2.

— Niki Kelly (@nkellyIN) November 4, 2026.

The vote also lands in a state that is narrowing gambling elsewhere. House Bill 1052 lets the commission fine any operator or individual $100,000 for knowingly running an internet sweepstakes game in Indiana, starting July 1, 2026. Peer-to-peer skill-based poker is exempt. Indiana still has no legal online casinos.

Indiana was not alone on Election Day, as Nebraska voters also turned down a gambling expansion. In northeast Indiana, the act’s December 1, 2026 deadline for inland casino license applications now arrives with the commission taking no applications.

  • Both cases allege illegal gambling and violations of the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin has sued sweepstakes casino operator VGW and prediction market Kalshi on the same day, alleging illegal gambling under state law. The VGW complaint puts a dollar figure on the state's sweepstakes market and adds Arkansas to a growing list of states challenging the dual-currency model.

In a recent development, arkansas has opened a two-front legal fight against online gambling it says is unlicensed. One lawsuit targets VGW, the company behind Chumba Casino, LuckyLand and Global Poker. The other targets KalshiEX LLC and Kalshi Inc., the companies that own the Kalshi prediction market.

Both cases allege illegal gambling and violations of the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Both also include an unjust enrichment claim. In each case the state seeks restitution, penalties, taxes and injunctive relief.

The VGW suit attacks the Gold Coin/Sweeps Coin model that almost every US sweepstakes casino relies on. It names ten affiliated VGW companies. The complaint indicates VGW reported about $66 million in taxable Arkansas sales between July 2025 and June 2026 and paid about $6 million in sales and use tax over that period, Gaming.net reported.

Industry observers note that those figures show a firm declaring sales to the state and paying tax on them. Yet VGW holds no Arkansas casino license, the state alleges. The complaint also accuses VGW of letting 18-year-olds play, even though Arkansas casinos require players to be 21.

According to recent reports, the case lands less than two months after the Newly introduced York settlement. New York Attorney General Letitia James announced that deal on September 9, 2026. It covered Chumba Casino, Global Poker and Luckyland Slots. VGW’s coin-based games were already off the table for New Yorkers by then, after her office sent the company a cease-and-desist letter in June 2025.

Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman went to court a few months earlier, claiming VGW’s sweepstakes casinos break Kentucky gambling law. Florida has also moved against dual-currency sweepstakes since June 2026. Arkansas now joins Kentucky, Florida and Latest York on that list. For operators using the same coin structure, the pattern points to rising legal exposure state by state.

In a recent development, the Kalshi complaint rests on a constitutional definition. The Arkansas Constitution’s definition of casino gaming expressly covers accepting wagers on sporting events. Kalshi has never held a casino-gaming license from the state commission, the state alleges. Nor has it held any other Arkansas authorization to take sports wagers.

The complaint expressly limits itself to state-law claims and relief under Arkansas law. That choice means the state is relying on its own consumer-protection statute rather than waiting on the CFTC. Money lost, betting that gets out of hand, and depression or other damage to mental health are dangers Kalshi understands its customers face, Griffin’s office said.

Today I filed a lawsuit against VGW, an online gaming platform that features such games as @ChumbaCasino, LuckyLand Casino, @LuckyLandSlots, and @official_glp.

According to recent reports, arkansas’s gambling laws are clear. If you’re providing a means for Arkansans to gamble money within our state, you are… pic.twitter.com/qs2dhRMC8K.

— Attorney General Tim Griffin (@AGTimGriffin) November 4, 2026.

It has been revealed that filing both cases on the same day signals how Arkansas views the two products. The attorney general is treating sweepstakes casinos and sports event contracts as the same kind of unlicensed gambling. Other states may weigh whether to copy that approach.

According to recent reports, the VGW case was filed in White County Circuit Court. The Kalshi case was filed in Independence County Circuit Court.
