Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I help lead Google's agent skills program, currently with 175 agent skills that supplement community collections like go-skills.
  • Recent findings suggest that in Go, every slice or index operation that can panic at runtime compiles down to an explicit bounds-check trap in machine code, after the compiler's optimizer strips out the checks it can already rule out.
  • In this post, I'll walk through how the Gemini and Z3 pipeline works, why go test -fuzz missed two of those crashes (and the one-line change that fixes it), and where this approach fits in a day-to-day Go workflow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I help lead Google's agent skills program, currently with 175 agent skills that supplement community collections like go-skills. To keep that many skill files consistent, I wrote skill-lint, a standalone Go CLI that checks SKILL.md files and applies LLM-generated line edits before they ship. Even with skill-lint's own unit and fuzz test suite, a small slice or line-number mistake inside its Markdown parsers or edit applier can sit dormant until an unusual file or edit range triggers a runtime panic in the linter.

Recent findings suggest that in Go, every slice or index operation that can panic at runtime compiles down to an explicit bounds-check trap in machine code, after the compiler's optimizer strips out the checks it can already rule out. To hunt for crashes, I compiled key functions from my code to see which panic traps survived optimization, and Gemini 4 Argon translated the path to each trap into rules for the Z3 constraint solver. An LLM-written solver model isn't a sound proof system, but it gives the agent an independent way to reason about control flow and synthesize concrete Go reproducers, and every crash it finds is real because go test runs the offending bytes directly. That workflow caught all three bugs I planted in test parsers and turned up three latent bugs in skill-lint.

In this post, I'll walk through how the Gemini and Z3 pipeline works, why go test -fuzz missed two of those crashes (and the one-line change that fixes it), and where this approach fits in a day-to-day Go workflow.

Recent findings suggest that A recent post from Anthropic showed how formal verification catches latent bugs in C and C++ by having frontier AI models write machine-checked Rocq proofs across OSS-Fuzz libraries. Instead of sampling random inputs like a fuzzer, a formal tool works backward from each failure condition to solve for the exact input that triggers it. Full theorem proving is still too heavy for most day-to-day Go projects, so I wanted to see how much of that bug-hunting power an agent can get from an LLM and a constraint solver in about a minute per function.

In C and C++, reading or writing past the end of a buffer corrupts memory. Go catches out-of-bounds access at runtime instead, compiling every slice or index operation it can't prove safe into an explicit branch to runtime.panicBounds that panics, crashing the process unless recovered.

In a recent development, before generating machine code, Go's SSA prove pass already eliminates most of those checks by tracking slice lengths and loop variables. That optimization pass leaves behind only the runtime.panicBounds traps the compiler couldn't rule out on its own, giving the solver a short list of candidate crash sites to target.

Recent findings suggest that I compiled each target with GOOS=linux GOARCH=riscv64 go build -gcflags="-S -d=ssa/check_bce/debug=1" (-S prints the assembly listing and ssa/check_bce/debug=1 logs every surviving bounds check) and passed both the Go source and the disassembly to the model. Looking at Go source alone, you can't see which bounds checks the compiler already removed or where a register gets truncated to 8 bits; in the disassembly, both show up. I targeted RISC-V because it's the instruction set Anthropic's post targets for its Rocq proofs, and Go cross-compiles to it out of the box.

According to recent reports, from there, Argon read the Go source and disassembly and returned a Z3 script modeling the path to each surviving trap, along with a patched function whenever it flagged a bug. Z3 then checked whether those constraints could be satisfied, and whenever it found a crashing input, go test replayed those bytes against the real function. Using an LLM saved me from translating assembly into solver constraints by hand. Argon's translation dominated the runtime, at about a minute per function, while Z3 itself finished in milliseconds.

By the way, before we dive in, Mat Marquis’ highly recommended JavaScript for Everyone course is currently -30% off (code: CSSTRICKSFRIENDS). You don’t want to miss this.

Preethi Sam demonstrated how to create background image refraction effects with CSS. The effects are stunning, can be animated, don’t need very much CSS (no JavaScript), and we don’t need to duplicate the image either.

Brecht De Ruyte demonstrated how to build customizable components using container style queries and advanced attr(), showcasing some incredible interactive demos, including the two below:.

In a recent development, dan Holloran indicated us how to use the different scroll-state() queries (scrollable, scrolled, snapped, and stuck). It’s not a long read, which is exactly what you want for a fresh but simple feature like this.

A quick, no-context CSS snippet to entice you:.

Declan Chidlow shared some of the craziest CSS to ever exist, and I mean craziest. Most of it comes from Internet Explorer, but let’s face it, you knew that already. Thankfully, they don’t build them like they used to.

According to recent reports, bramus demonstrated how to animate CSS grids using anchor positioning. The idea is that we anchor content to its corresponding cell, and then as the grid reflows, it’s the content (not the cell) that animates with it.

(But it doesn’t work in Firefox due to what sounds like a bug.).

According to recent reports, chris Coyier talked about a bunch of upcoming HTML features, and honestly, there’s a whole lot in there that you definitely haven’t heard of. Like, I’m certain of it.

Recent findings suggest that victor Ayomipo contemplated why container query adoption has been so terrible despite them topping CSS wishlists for years. Victor thinks that we’re using them wrong, so he’s here to set the record straight.

Cory LaViska demonstrated how to use @custom-media in addition to container style queries as a fallback.

Also, don’t forget that Declan has an extremely thorough @custom-media deep-dive in our Almanac.

Recent findings suggest that ahmad Shadeed tackled an interesting topic — detecting overlapping elements (with CSS, of course). If you’re keen on anchor positioning, scroll-driven animations, and again (!), container style queries, then this walkthrough is for you.

I want to know when the decorative element hits the section from the left edge, taking into consideration that the element might have a fluid position or size that changes with the viewport size or container size. Basically, it’s a dynamic problem. It’s not about using a media query to hide the decorative element, I want to hide it upon overlapping.

Maybe container queries are finally picking up?

Sources indicate that patrick Brosset walked us through a proposal for the previewsrc HTML attribute, which would enable us to supply preview images for images that haven’t yet loaded using only HTML. For example, we could supply a blurry preview image. However, I’d rather have something like :loaded/:not(:loaded) so that we can style/transition unloaded images with CSS rather than needing to create extra images.

Temani Afif shared a custom borders demo, where the trick is to declare a transparent border, use border-shape to define its shape, then declare a background in addition to background-clip: border-area so that it only indicates up within the border, like this (requires Chrome at the moment):.

In a similar manner, Leon Arnott shared this awesome trick for animating the background color of ::selection, something that’s actually forbidden (or so we thought, anyway…):.

Recent findings suggest that today in CSS: We all know you can change the highlight colour of selected text, but it's impossible to animate that colour. Unless… the colour was just a variable inherited from the parent element, using @​property to make it animatable… Hahahahaha… [image or embed].

And that’s it, really. Simply use var(--bg-color) on ::selection or some other visually restrictive element.

Sources indicate that chris Coyier demonstrated how to random()ly animate an element along the edge of another element. There’s a cute doggo, by the way. Probably should’ve led with that.

Polypane explained how we might disable the root scroller accidentally (which is surprisingly easy to do — I’ve definitely done it), what we lose in doing so, and what to do instead.

Sources indicate that also, have you ever completely misunderstood how the root (:root/html) works? This is a solid explainer for that, too.

Speaking of accidents, have you ever tapped on a target twice, apparently in quick succession, and ended up zooming in? Andy Bell revealed that touch-action: manipulation disables the double-tap-to-zoom-in functionality. It isn’t upcoming, but I don’t see many web developers using it. One for the CSS reset, I think?

Chrome and Firefox now ship every two weeks. The inaugural releases were fairly exciting (not smaller, as I assumed they’d be). In addition, Safari 27 (along with iOS, iPadOS, and macOS 27) shipped with some of the same features as Firefox, making them Baseline in the same release window. High fives all around!

And, as always, thanks for tuning in!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that fanDuel's US adjusted EBITDA nearly disappeared in the third quarter of 2026, even as US revenue rose 6%. Flutter blamed spending on FanDuel Predicts and its Alberta launch, while FanDuel Casino's revenue growth slowed to 8%.

In a recent development, fanDuel’s US business barely turned a profit in the third quarter of 2026. US adjusted EBITDA came in at just $3 million, against $51 million a year earlier. Revenue moved the other way, climbing 6% to $1.455 billion. Flutter blamed spending on FanDuel Predicts and its launch in Alberta.

For the regulated US market, the result highlights how much prediction-market spending is costing one of its online leaders. The parent firm also lowered its full-year outlook for 2026. Buybacks are on hold for the foreseeable future so Flutter can focus on organic investment and paying down debt. Leverage stood at 4.6x at the end of the quarter, up from 3.7x in December 2025.

In a recent development, the group’s net loss widened to $1.148 billion from $789 million a year earlier. That figure includes impairments tied to Brazil, where Flutter stopped operating on Sept. 26, 2026.

FanDuel Casino is adding players much faster than it is adding revenue. Flutter pointed to competition and to slower growth as US iGaming states mature. The contrast with late 2025 is sharp. In the fourth quarter of 2025, FanDuel Casino grew revenue 33% and held 28% of US iGaming gross gaming revenue.

In a recent development, flutter put that share at 27% for the three months to Sept. 30, the same level it reported for the second quarter. An outside estimate is lower. FanDuel’s iGaming share was 25.1%, down from 26.6% a year earlier, according to Citizens figures published by NEXT.io. The same figures revealed US iGaming growth slowing to 12% year over year in the third quarter, the lowest on record.

In a recent development, sportsbook revenue grew 4%. FanDuel’s share of US sportsbook gross gaming revenue slipped to 36%, from 39% in the second quarter. Its share of handle was 33%.

In a recent development, the product drawing the investment is gaining consumers. Trading volume on FanDuel Predicts rose 102% from the prior quarter to $119 million. CEO Dan Taylor remarked the app had 140,000 active users in October.

Flutter reiterates $50m prediction market revenue target for 2026:.

Flutter's FanDuel Predicts reached 140,000 active people in October as its parent maintained its $40m adjusted EBITDA forecast for market-making.

Full Story ➡️ https://t.co/B7KSlEgH0a pic.twitter.com/zKXX8fV2fG.

— NEXTpredict (@nextpredictio) November 4, 2026.

Industry observers note that alberta is the other latest cost. FanDuel reached more than 20% of the gaming market there in its first quarter. Management mentioned that was well ahead of its pace after launching in Ontario.

Sources indicate that together, the figures are consistent with a firm trading near-term US profit for growth in newer markets and products. Taylor took over as CEO from Peter Jackson on Oct. 1, 2026. Buybacks will stay paused until leverage falls to a range of 2 to 2.5 times, a target he set for a period of about 24 months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Something wicked this way comes.”.

According to recent reports, it was naivety, but when I first came across Flexbox, and then CSS Grid, I had this feeling all those positioning properties (align-self, justify-content…) would be available to use on block and inline elements; things like tables, lists, fixed elements, everything. The workings might be different under the hood, depending on the reference boxes, but the syntax and expected outcomes would be same: push to one edge, keep at the center, spread around evenly, etc.

Although that didn’t happen, what if I made something of that sort?

For example, I could take out the soul of an HTML table and stitch it back together with CSS Grid. In other words, it reads like a table, but acts like a grid, allowing me to use grid properties. Believe it or not, some form of this was used in the past to make tables responsive.

Before I kill off a table in this article though: there are a lot of advantages to straight-up tables. They provide a clean semantic layout that browsers perfectly understand and translate for assistive technology when needed. There’s even a element.

According to recent reports, on the CSS side of things, there are indeed circumstances where CSS Grid is necessary for its intrinsic responsiveness, source order independence, and positioning. That’s why it’s an indispensable tool for layouts. Use that and let HTML tables to do the work of actually displaying tabular data!

But there’s the presentational benefit of table we should consider. Technically, is not a presentational element like a . It’s semantic: the browser and I share a common meaning for it. But whether the browser understands it as such or not, if I read I believe it’s a heading followed by data. Let’s say that’s pseudo-semantic to me, if presentation is not the right term.

That pseudo-semanticism is still useful. It’s the difference between me having to read this:.

Despite there being semantic elements for titles, like and , they don’t bring in the connection that and have, and it’s better to reserve and for textual structuring like glossaries rather than layouts.

Recent findings suggest that so, is it okay if I use this way? I mean, the table itself merely used as pseudo-semantic markup skin:.

Then, this CSS and its outcome (for the first markup):.

…changes to this (for the table markup):.

To me, the latter markup example — a pseudo-semantic table — is easier to scan than a handful of generic divs. I get the pseudo-semantics of table, and the ease of using CSS Grid for the layout. As for browsers, none of them have shunned this sort of Frankenstein creation, at least yet. The VoiceOver and keyboard navigation works as if it’s a real table.

Recent findings suggest that but it’s understandable why it looks more than a little gross and against the grain of what we should be able to. We’re encouraged to maintain a separation of concerns between content and presentation and this does exactly that without affecting the tables semantics, such as its role. But maybe it should? There are plenty of other HTML elements that CSS is capable of busting.

Your AI Pipeline Works. But Can You Trust It?

It has been revealed that AI is becoming a part of almost everything we do in technology today. Whether it's detecting fraudulent transactions, assessing credit risk, forecasting demand, or personalizing customer experiences, organizations are increasingly relying on AI to make faster and smarter decisions.

And naturally, when we talk about building AI systems, most of the conversation revolves around model accuracy, performance, and deployment. We spend considerable time making sure our models are trained well, our pipelines run efficiently, and our systems can handle production workloads.

But here's something we don't always pay enough attention to: Can we actually trust the data feeding these models?

After all, even the most sophisticated AI model can produce misleading results if the underlying data is incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrectly interpreted. What's interesting is that these problems don't always show up as technical failures. Sometimes, everything appears to be working perfectly fine.

Imagine a financial institution that has recently deployed an AI-powered loan risk assessment system. The team has spent months preparing the data, training the model, testing its performance, and finally moving it into production.

Sources indicate that the deployment goes smoothly. Data pipelines are running on schedule, predictions are being generated, and all the monitoring dashboards are green.

In a recent development, A few weeks later, however, the business team notices something unusual. The model has started classifying more customers as high risk than expected.

Industry observers note that the data science team checks the model configuration. Nothing has changed. The engineering team reviews the pipelines. All jobs have completed successfully. Even the infrastructure looks healthy.

It turns out that an upstream source system changed the definition of a customer income field from annual gross income to annual net income. The field name remained the same, the data type was still numeric, and none of the existing technical validations detected the change.

The pipeline continued running as expected, but the model was now receiving information with a different business meaning.

This brings us to an key point: Just because an AI pipeline runs successfully doesn't necessarily mean we can trust its output.

In a recent development, building reliable AI systems requires us to look beyond the model itself. We need to understand where the data originates, how it changes as it moves through different systems, whether it meets quality expectations, and who is responsible when something goes wrong.

In this article, we'll explore three key elements of trustworthy AI pipelines (data quality, data lineage, and accountability) and look at how engineering teams can incorporate them into their existing workflows without making the process unnecessarily complicated.

In a recent development, most modern data pipelines come with some form of operational monitoring. Engineering teams track job completion, execution time, system availability, and processing failures.

These metrics are crucial because they help us understand whether our systems are functioning as expected.

Industry observers note that operational monitoring primarily tells us whether a pipeline executed successfully. It doesn't necessarily tell us whether the data being processed is accurate, consistent, or suitable for the model consuming it.

Suppose we're building a loan risk model that uses a customer's debt-to-income ratio as one of its input features.

The calculation is straightforward:.

Debt-to-income ratio = Monthly debt payments / Monthly income.

Now imagine that an upstream system starts supplying annual income instead of monthly income.

According to recent reports, the calculation still executes successfully. The values are numeric, the transformation doesn't throw an error, and the model continues generating predictions.

However, the resulting debt-to-income ratio is incorrect because the numerator and denominator represent different time periods.

This is where traditional monitoring falls short.

To build trustworthy AI pipelines, we need to look at different dimensions of system health.

These approaches complement each other.

According to recent reports, A pipeline can be operationally healthy while processing unreliable data. Similarly, a model can continue producing predictions even when the meaning of an crucial input field has changed.

For engineering teams, the objective should be to identify these problems as early as possible, ideally before they reach downstream models.

We've all heard the phrase "garbage in, garbage out.".

And despite all the progress we've made in artificial intelligence, this principle hasn't changed.

AI models may be capable of processing enormous volumes of data and identifying complex patterns, but they cannot automatically guarantee that the information they're receiving is correct.

This is where data quality becomes important.

Data quality refers to how well information meets the requirements of its intended use. In AI pipelines, it helps us determine whether incoming data is sufficiently reliable for model training, evaluation, or inference.

Let's look at four dimensions that are particularly relevant.

Imagine we're developing a loan risk model that relies on customer income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

What happens if 20% of the incoming records are missing income information?

According to recent reports, should we reject those records? Should we replace missing values using an approved statistical method? Or should we flag them for additional review?

There isn't one answer that works for every system.

The right approach depends on the model, the business requirements, and the potential consequences of the decision.

What matters is that missing information is handled deliberately.

For example, replacing missing income with zero may allow the pipeline to continue running, but it could significantly distort the model's predictions.

Validity checks whether values meet expected formats, ranges, and business rules.

Consider a customer record containing the following information:.

The credit utilization value immediately stands out.

Although credit utilization can exceed 100% in certain circumstances, a value of 450% may warrant investigation.

This highlights an key distinction: Not every unusual value is incorrect, and not every technically valid value is meaningful.

A database may accept any numeric value, but the business may need additional rules to determine whether that value is appropriate for the model.

Engineering teams should distinguish between invalid records, unexpected observations, and legitimate exceptions.

This is one of the most common challenges in enterprise data environments.

Imagine two systems providing customer income information.

System A reports annual gross income.

System B reports monthly net income.

Both datasets contain a column called income.

If we combine these datasets without understanding their definitions, we risk introducing inconsistencies into downstream calculations.

Industry observers note that the data may look perfectly fine from a technical perspective. The problem is that the same field represents different business concepts.

This is why data definitions, units, and transformation rules are just as important as schema validation.

Suppose a model predicts a customer's current financial risk using income information that was last updated 18 months ago.

The data might be accurate, complete, and consistent.

But is it current enough to support the decision?

Different AI applications have different freshness requirements.

A real-time fraud detection model may require near-real-time transaction information, while a long-term forecasting model may work with less frequently updated datasets.

The important thing is to define these expectations based on how the data will be used.

The good news is that improving data quality doesn't always require sophisticated enterprise tools.

A practical starting point is to define validation rules for the most notable input fields.

For example, consider the following conceptual configuration:.

This is an illustrative data quality contract rather than executable configuration for a particular framework.

It defines basic expectations and specifies what should happen when the data fails validation.

It has been revealed that tools such as Great Expectations can help automate these checks. For smaller systems, custom SQL or Python validations may be sufficient.

However, technical validation alone isn't enough.

Remember our original example where the income field changed from gross to net income?

Both values could easily pass a rule requiring income to be greater than zero.

Detecting that kind of problem requires clear business definitions, communication with upstream systems, and appropriate change management.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, data quality isn't just about checking values. It's also about understanding what those values represent.

Now let's assume our loan risk model generates an unexpectedly high risk score for a customer.

The model output is available, but we want to understand what contributed to the prediction.

We start investigating the input data.

The income information came from a customer application system. Outstanding debt came from another database. Both datasets went through several transformations before reaching the feature engineering pipeline.

The final features were then passed to the model.

At this point, a seemingly simple question becomes surprisingly difficult:.

Where exactly did the information used for this prediction come from?

This is where data lineage becomes valuable.

Data lineage describes how data originates, moves, and changes across different systems.

For AI pipelines, it helps us understand the journey from raw source data to the features used by a model.

A simplified flow might look like this:.

Source Systems → Data Transformation → Feature Engineering → Model Inference → Predictions.

Each stage introduces dependencies that can affect downstream results.

Data lineage can be captured at different levels of detail.

Dataset-level lineage reveals relationships between datasets.

Loan Applications → Cleaned Applications → Model Features.

This helps us understand how datasets move through the overall architecture.

However, suppose the model's debt-to-income ratio suddenly changes.

Dataset-level lineage might tell us which datasets were involved, but it may not provide enough detail to identify the affected field.

That's where column-level lineage becomes useful.

debt_to_income_ratio = monthly_debt_payment / monthly_income.

Column-level lineage can show that the resulting feature depends on two upstream attributes.

If one of those attributes changes, engineers can trace the dependency and investigate the impact.

This is especially valuable in environments where multiple reports, applications, and AI models depend on shared data sources.

Large organizations may use dedicated metadata management and lineage platforms.

However, smaller teams can start by capturing essential metadata during pipeline execution.

OpenLineage provides an open standard for collecting and exchanging lineage metadata across supported systems.

For more detailed prediction-level investigations, teams may also need to retain feature snapshots or inference logs, subject to privacy and retention requirements.

It's important to understand that lineage doesn't automatically guarantee data accuracy.

A pipeline can be perfectly documented and still contain incorrect transformation logic.

But when something goes wrong, lineage gives engineering teams a clearer starting point for investigation.

Instead of searching across multiple systems and trying to reconstruct dependencies manually, they can identify where data originated and how it changed along the way.

Let's consider another situation.

An AI model starts producing unexpected results.

The data science team checks the model and finds no concerns.

The data engineering team confirms that the pipelines are running successfully.

The source-system team verifies that data was delivered according to its interface.

Yet the problem remains unresolved.

Everyone has completed their individual checks, but nobody has identified who should coordinate the investigation.

This is where accountability becomes notable.

Industry observers note that AI pipelines often involve multiple teams responsible for different stages of the data lifecycle. Without clearly defined ownership, even relatively simple issues can take longer to resolve.

A practical accountability framework should distinguish between three responsibilities.

Data owners are responsible for defining the business meaning and expected quality of critical information.

For example, someone needs to determine whether an income field represents gross income, net income, or another financial measure.

These definitions should be documented and communicated to downstream consumers.

Data engineering and platform teams typically manage data ingestion, transformations, validation mechanisms, and pipeline operations.

Their responsibilities may include implementing quality checks, monitoring failures, and assessing the technical impact of changes.

However, technical teams shouldn't be expected to make business-definition decisions without appropriate input.

Data science and ML engineering teams are responsible for evaluating model behavior, managing model versions, and assessing how changes in input data may affect predictions.

If a critical feature changes, the model team may need to determine whether additional testing, recalibration, or retraining is required.

Defining ownership is useful, but connecting it to an operational process is even more important.

Consider a critical data quality failure during feature generation.

A response process might look like this:.

The exact workflow will vary depending on the organization and the risk associated with the application.

The objective is to ensure that technical alerts lead to clear actions.

After all, an alert that nobody owns is just another notification waiting to be ignored.

So far, we've discussed why data quality, lineage, and accountability matter.

But how can we bring these concepts into everyday engineering practices?

Here are five controls that teams can introduce without redesigning their entire architecture.

Data contracts define expectations between data producers and consumers.

They can document schemas, field definitions, units, freshness requirements, and compatibility expectations.

For example, rather than specifying only that annual_income is numeric, a contract should clarify whether it represents gross or net income, the currency, and the applicable time period.

This reduces the risk of downstream systems misinterpreting technically valid information.

Quality gates validate critical data before it progresses through the pipeline.

These checks can be implemented during ingestion, transformation, feature generation, or inference.

For example, a feature engineering process calculating debt-to-income ratios should verify that debt and income values use compatible time periods.

In a recent development, failure handling should reflect the severity of the issue. Some records may be quarantined, while more serious failures may require stopping the pipeline.

Pipeline execution should produce sufficient metadata to identify source datasets, transformations, and downstream outputs.

Where appropriate, teams should also capture model and feature versions associated with predictions.

This information supports impact analysis, debugging, and investigation when unexpected results occur.

AI systems evolve continuously.

Datasets change, transformation logic is updated, features are modified, and models are retrained.

Versioning helps engineering teams understand which components were active at a particular point in time.

Relevant evidence may include pipeline configurations, dataset snapshots, model versions, validation outcomes, and deployment records.

Retention should be designed around operational requirements, privacy considerations, and applicable policies rather than storing everything indefinitely.

Every critical data element or pipeline component should have an identified owner or responsible team.

More importantly, ownership should connect directly to incident management and change approval processes.

If a source definition changes, teams should know who evaluates the impact.

If a quality gate fails, the responsible team should receive the alert.

If model performance deteriorates, the investigation should have a clear escalation path.

These controls are most effective when they become part of normal development and deployment practices rather than separate administrative activities.

Implementing comprehensive governance across an entire data environment can be challenging, particularly for organizations with legacy systems and complex dependencies.

A more effective approach is to begin with one critical AI pipeline.

For example, a team operating a loan risk model could start by identifying the inputs that have the greatest influence on its predictions.

These might include income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

For each critical input, the team can document five things:.

Once these foundations are established, the team can implement automated checks and gradually extend the approach to additional datasets.

This incremental strategy also makes it easier to demonstrate the value of governance controls.

For instance, teams can track how promptly data-related incidents are detected, how long investigations take, and whether recurring issues are reduced.

The goal isn't to introduce governance for its own sake.

It's to improve the reliability, maintainability, and transparency of the systems developers are responsible for operating.

Explainable AI has become an crucial topic in machine learning.

Techniques such as feature importance analysis and SHAP can help teams understand which inputs influence model predictions.

However, explainability and data trustworthiness address different problems.

Suppose a model explanation identifies debt-to-income ratio as a major contributor to a customer's high-risk classification.

That explanation may accurately describe the model's behavior.

But if the debt-to-income ratio was calculated using an incorrectly defined income field, the explanation alone may not reveal the underlying data glitch.

This highlights the importance of evaluating AI systems across multiple dimensions.

Model explainability helps us understand how predictions are generated.

Data quality helps establish whether inputs satisfy defined expectations.

Data lineage provides visibility into where information originated and how it was transformed.

Accountability ensures that identified problems can be investigated and addressed.

These capabilities are complementary rather than interchangeable.

None independently guarantees that an AI system is accurate, fair, secure, or compliant. Together, however, they provide a stronger foundation for evaluating and improving system reliability.

As AI systems become more integrated into business processes, engineering teams face increasing expectations around reliability, transparency, and accountability.

Model accuracy and operational performance remain essential, but they represent only part of the overall picture.

A pipeline can execute successfully while processing inconsistent information. A model can generate predictions using features whose definitions have changed. And an explanation can describe a model's behavior without identifying problems in the underlying data.

Building trustworthy AI therefore requires attention to the entire data lifecycle.

Data quality controls help detect unreliable inputs. Lineage provides visibility into how information moves through systems. Clear ownership ensures that complications can be investigated and resolved.

Importantly, these practices don't need to begin with large-scale governance programs or expensive technology investments.

Engineering teams can start with a single critical pipeline, identify its most crucial data elements, establish quality expectations, and introduce basic traceability and accountability mechanisms.

Over time, these practices can become part of standard development and deployment workflows.

The real measure of a trustworthy AI pipeline isn't simply whether it produces a prediction. It's whether the organization can understand, validate, and take responsibility for the information behind that prediction.

After all, a green dashboard is reassuring. But it shouldn't be the only evidence that an AI system is working as intended.

This is the final glitch of What’s !vital on CSS-Tricks.com. The good news is that it’s coming back in an expanded form as the CSS-Tricks newsletter. I had ya there for a second, didn’t I? Sorry, I couldn’t decide whether to trick or treat, so I went for both. Happy Halloween!

Recent findings suggest that the newsletter officially kicks off on November 10th. That’s after a way-too-long four-year hiatus. What the heck, right? It’s not only high time for it to come back, but for you to get on the list. You’ll get hand-written and hand-curated news, links, and editorials that you can only find there. Join the party with me!

So, let’s go out with a big bang for our “final” issue. It’s packed with some stuff that I’ve been holding onto since before the site came back to life earlier this week, but also some new stuff, and I can’t wait to finally get it out to you.

Scooch over Apple, Rockstar has something they’d like to say about fancy scrolling effects (to be fair, they’ve had 13 years to create them). First, check out the GTA 6 website (which oddly doesn’t work in Firefox), then watch Kevin Powell’s GTA 6 scroll effects walkthrough, which is frankly the most fun that you can have while waiting (and waiting) for GTA 6.

Mojtaba Seyedi demonstrated how to build a scrollspy with modern CSS. What’s a scrollspy, you ask? Well, if you have a navigation that links to different sections of the page, a scrollspy highlights the section that you’re currently on in the navigation.

Brecht De Ruyte showcased and explained some absolutely stunning random() demos.

Okay, that was more than a few….

Lea Verou explained, in detail, the different ways of implementing icons on the web. Many exciting CSS features of the future are mentioned, including Linked Parameters, ident(), @mixin and @apply, the @property shorthand, and more, so it’s a really deep dive with a lot of intrigue.

Kilian Valkhof suggested a universal pseudo-selector. I mean, the universal selector (*) doesn’t select pseudo-elements, which is why almost every website uses the following CSS snippet, right?

But there are way more of them now (e.g., ::backdrop and ::details-content, to name just a couple of common ones in the context of box-sizing: border-box), so Kilian suggests ::*.

Declan Chidlow told us which newly introduced HTML and CSS features are useful for design systems. My favorites are text-box, sibling-index(), sibling-count(), @scope, and @custom-media, which are very handy even outside of design systems.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • PENN Entertainment's online segment grew revenue in the third quarter, but the gain came from passed-through partner gaming taxes, not from players.
  • Other revenues carried the whole of the Interactive segment’s third-quarter gain at PENN Entertainment.
  • This pattern places PENN within the slowing-iGaming-growth story running through this week’s US operator reports.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PENN Entertainment's online segment grew revenue in the third quarter, but the gain came from passed-through partner gaming taxes, not from players. The segment now needs a positive fourth quarter to reach a full-year target that has already been lowered.

Other revenues carried the whole of the Interactive segment’s third-quarter gain at PENN Entertainment. Segment revenue rose to $348.4 million from $297.7 million, while the third-party partner gaming-tax amounts booked there climbed to $191.4 million from $139.5 million a year earlier. Online gaming revenue itself fell 2.1% to $126.6 million from $129.3 million, as iCasino growth was offset by lower sports betting handle.

This pattern places PENN within the slowing-iGaming-growth story running through this week’s US operator reports.

Recent findings suggest that the nine-month figures show the same reliance on the gross-up. Interactive revenue reached $1,056.0 million, up from $903.9 million. The tax gross-up within it rose to $562.7 million from $405.6 million.

Sources indicate that the group as a whole had a stronger quarter. Total revenue was $1,840.0 million. Net income came in at $32.6 million, against a $865.1 million net loss a year earlier. PENN also raised its full-year retail guidance to $5.89 billion in revenue and $1.973 billion in adjusted EBITDAR, increases of $16 million and $10 million.

Industry observers note that profitability is improving faster than revenue. The Interactive adjusted EBITDA loss for the first nine months shrank to $38.7 million from $227.6 million. PENN attributes that mainly to lower marketing, general and administrative, and labor costs.

Expansion has weighed on the quarter. PENN launched theScore Bet, theScore Casino and standalone Hollywood iCasino apps in Alberta on July 13, 2026. Excluding that third-quarter launch investment, Interactive adjusted EBITDA improved quarter over quarter throughout 2026, management said on the earnings call.

According to recent reports, the standalone Hollywood iCasino brand is central to the proposal. It posted record quarterly revenue in the second quarter. PENN is now leaning on its US growth, and on steady trends through October, to support the full-year Interactive target. That makes the brand a test for whether a mid-tier US online casino can turn profitable.

The target itself has moved. In February, PENN guided the segment to breakeven adjusted EBITDA for 2026, which it described as a $268 million improvement from 2025. The cost of the Alberta launch is now built into a weaker outlook.

PENN Entertainment CEO Jay Snowden discussed the potential of more Canadian provinces launching iGaming on an earnings call today.

In the last month, Quebec, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia have all shown interest in exploring commercial online gambling.https://t.co/8WqAPfw9LY.

— Tom Nightingale (@TNightingaming) November 5, 2026.

It has been revealed that land-based trends offer some support. CEO Jay Snowden noted PENN’s own Pennsylvania gaming revenue in October posted stronger year-over-year growth than in any other month of 2026. Most of that growth came in the second half of the month, after skill games were shut down. In his view, the midterm results could help PENN further by weakening support for skill-game machines.

Recent findings suggest that the online segment still has to deliver. Reaching the revised target depends on Interactive turning its third-quarter loss into positive adjusted EBITDA in the fourth quarter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Second Circuit has refused to shield Kalshi and Coinbase from Upcoming York and Connecticut while their appeals proceed.
  • A federal appeals panel has left Kalshi and Coinbase without interim protection in two Northeastern states.
  • The ruling came a few hours after the panel heard lawyers for Kalshi, Coinbase, the CFTC, Fresh York and Connecticut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Second Circuit has refused to shield Kalshi and Coinbase from Upcoming York and Connecticut while their appeals proceed. The ruling lets both states press state-court cases against the companies' sports event contracts and deepens a circuit split headed for the Supreme Court.

A federal appeals panel has left Kalshi and Coinbase without interim protection in two Northeastern states. The Second Circuit found that the companies had not made the showing needed for an injunction pending appeal. The order did not say which part of that showing they failed to meet.

The ruling came a few hours after the panel heard lawyers for Kalshi, Coinbase, the CFTC, Fresh York and Connecticut. The court took up Kalshi’s two appeals together with Coinbase’s appeal of Judge Oliver’s August decision. That decision allowed Connecticut to keep pursuing its claim that Coinbase’s sports event contracts are illegal gambling.

The order lets both states keep enforcing their gambling laws. They are pursuing state-court suits to force the sports event contracts offline. Gaming attorney Daniel Wallach called the ruling a major win for both states. He mentioned one remand order now separates them from returning the cases to state court and seeking preliminary injunctions there.

Industry observers note that kalshi had already lost at the district level. Federal courts refused it a preliminary injunction in New York in July and in Connecticut in August. On July 31, 2026, New York sued KalshiEX, accusing it of running an illegal gambling operation through its prediction market. Attorney General Letitia James had sued Coinbase and Gemini in April 2026 on similar illegal gambling claims.

According to recent reports, the stakes in Upcoming York are high. InGame reported that the state case seeks billions of dollars in damages, and that the CFTC has told Kalshi to disobey the state-court order if it ever takes effect.

Connecticut moved earlier. In December 2025, the Gaming Division of its Department of Consumer Protection ordered Kalshi and two other sites to stop offering unlicensed online sports wagering. On August 26, 2026, Attorney General William Tong, Consumer Protection Commissioner Bryan T. Cafferelli and Gov. Ned Lamont revealed a lawsuit to stop Kalshi offering unlicensed sports wagers in the state. Gov. Kathy Hochul, James, Tong and Lamont each won re-election on the day the order was issued.

According to recent reports, the decision joins a lengthening list of circuit court rulings siding with states against prediction markets in 2026. It cuts against Kalshi’s argument that its contracts are “swaps” that only the CFTC can regulate. That argument prevailed at the Third Circuit, which ruled that Fresh Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets.

Nine federal judicial rulings within the Second Circuit have now gone against Kalshi, Coinbase and/or the CFTC in efforts to block state gambling enforcement through emergency or preliminary relief.

That includes today’s Second Circuit ruling denying Kalshi’s….

— Daniel Wallach (@WALLACHLEGAL) November 4, 2026.

According to recent reports, the federal regulator has also gone to court against states. On April 2, 2026, the CFTC sued Arizona, Connecticut and Illinois over their actions against CFTC-registered designated contract markets. On April 24, 2026, it sued Upcoming York in the Southern District of New York. It asked that court to declare that federal law gives it exclusive authority over event contracts. It also asked for a permanent bar on the state enforcing preempted laws.

The outcome matters for state sportsbook markets and for the reach of CFTC jurisdiction. With the circuits now split, attention turns to Washington. New Jersey’s petition seeks review of the Third Circuit’s April 6, 2026 decision in case 25-1922. Kalshi is preparing to file its response to that petition.

Geren reopens Texas casino fight, but his amendment still needs 21 Republican-led Senate votes

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readwrite

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Charlie Geren filed a constitutional amendment on the first filing day of Texas's 2027 session that would let voters decide on casinos and sports betting.
  • Texas lawmakers have their first gambling-expansion measures of the 2027 session.
  • The resolution would require lawmakers to limit casinos to a capped number of facilities statewide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Charlie Geren filed a constitutional amendment on the first filing day of Texas's 2027 session that would let voters decide on casinos and sports betting. A Democratic House and a supportive lieutenant governor-elect improve its odds, but a two-thirds Senate vote and a fight over the Senate's leadership stand in the way.

Texas lawmakers have their first gambling-expansion measures of the 2027 session. Rep. Charlie Geren, a Fort Worth Republican, filed House Joint Resolution 52 on November 9, the first day of bill filing, and Democratic Sen. Carol Alvarado filed a Senate resolution on casinos and sports betting, SJR 11, the same day. Voters would get the final say on a constitutional change giving lawmakers the power to permit and oversee casinos and sports betting.

The resolution would require lawmakers to limit casinos to a capped number of facilities statewide. Initial license terms would run at least 40 years. The Legislature would decide where sports betting could take place. The ballot wording would describe licensing, application fees and a tax on casino and sports wagering revenue at a limited number of locations.

Geren framed a statewide vote as the end of the debate either way. A rejection at the ballot box would close the question permanently, he noted.

The political ground has moved since Geren’s last attempt. Democrats won control of the Texas House in the November 3 election. Republicans held on to the Senate. As a state representative, Goodwin backed the 2023 gambling measure. The office she won was held by Dan Patrick, who blocked gambling expansion for years.

The constitutional route keeps the bar high. An amendment needs two-thirds of both chambers, then a majority of voters. Approved amendments go on the November ballot after the session ends. In 2023, online sports betting passed the House with 101 votes. Geren’s casino resolution reached only 92. The casino measure fell short of the threshold that the betting measure cleared.

The Senate is the harder test. Republicans control the chamber, and any amendment needs two-thirds support there. On November 9, Patrick urged Republican senators on conservative radio to strip Goodwin of her powers as Senate president before she takes office. Her influence over the chamber, including any gambling bill, now hangs on that fight.

Goodwin has signaled a conciliatory approach. Her transition team stated she wants to work with Republican senators and believes Texas is “best served by a deliberative, collaborative body.”.

According to recent reports, texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, arguably the casino and sports betting industry's biggest boogeyman in the Lone Star State, will leave office next year. What comes next in a crucial 2027 for the largest remaining state without major casino gaminghttps://t.co/u6WLlaAj3S.

— Ryan Butler (@butlerbetstrade) November 4, 2026.

It has been revealed that industry money has struggled to change the Republican map. In the March primaries, anti-gambling incumbents beat challengers backed by the Las Vegas Sands-funded Texas Sands PAC and Texas Defense PAC, to which Miriam Adelson had given $9 million. Even so, Texas Sands PAC has pledged to keep investing in and organizing for Texas candidates who favor bringing casino gambling to the state.

Sources indicate that that leaves Geren’s measure dependent on a Senate whose leadership is still contested. A simple majority could strip Goodwin’s powers once the chamber reconvenes in January.

Recent findings suggest that bally's North America Interactive unit grew revenue 25.6% in the third quarter of 2026, well ahead of a slowing US iGaming market, and narrowed its segment loss. The online unit still lost money, and the results came with another delayed quarterly filing after a going-concern warning in August.

Bally’s online business in the United States and Canada grew faster than the market in the third quarter. It is still not profitable. North America Interactive groups the company’s sports betting and iGaming businesses in both countries. The unit lost less money than a year earlier, but it stayed in the red.

The pace stands out against the wider market. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, according to Citizens JMP Securities. That was down from 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. Bally’s online growth ran well ahead of that slowing trend.

In a recent development, the quarter was not a clean step up, though. North America Interactive posted $66.1 million in second-quarter revenue, up 16.9% from a year earlier. Third-quarter sales were therefore lower than the quarter before. First-quarter revenue was $60.5 million, a 35.9% increase.

For the first nine months of 2026, the unit had preliminary revenue of $189.2 million. That compares with $134.0 million for February 8 to September 30, 2025, and $16.9 million for January 1 to February 7, 2025.

Recent findings suggest that A narrower loss points to progress. Yet the unit has not reached break-even, even while growing faster than the market. For a smaller US operator, online scale is still not translating into profit.

All third-quarter figures are preliminary. Bally’s has not finished closing its books for the period ended September 30, 2026, and the numbers could change. It filed a late-filing notice dated November 10 because it needed more time to finish reviewing its third-quarter financial statements.

Recent findings suggest that that makes three late quarterly reports in 2026. Bally’s notified the SEC in May that its first-quarter report would be late. It did the same in August for the second quarter. Both notices cited more time needed to review financial statements.

In the first-quarter 10-Q, management concluded that disclosure controls were not effective. The cause was a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting, first disclosed in the 2025 annual report.

The second-quarter 10-Q, filed August 14, went further. Two tests tied to the organization’s revolver, a net leverage covenant and a liquidity requirement, were expected to be missed during the coming year. That same filing carried a going-concern warning, questioning whether Bally’s could keep operating. The shares fell more than 25% in one trading session afterward.

Bally’s reports strong revenue growth in Q3 2026. Data and info: https://t.co/ekSd5Ngu0Q.

• Group revenue increased 22% to USD 807.6m, while North America Interactive revenue rose 26% to USD 62.7m.

Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1432 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset.
  • I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.
  • In a recent development, use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset. text-wrap: pretty can prevent a stranded word, container query units can scale a heading to the column it occupies, and text-box can trim the half-leading built into a line box. Some of these features are experimental and browser support is uneven, so they need guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.

In a recent development, use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you. I’ll walk you through all the details in this article and give you the full code at the end.

font-synthesis: none stops a browser from inventing bold or italic when the family lacks that face. The smoothing and text-rendering declarations are rendering hints, mainly for WebKit; results still vary by platform.

text-size-adjust disables mobile font inflation that can make a deliberately sized layout jump on rotation. font-size-adjust: from-font uses font metrics to reduce the apparent size change while a fallback swaps for a webfont.

(As with other snippets in this article, this ⁠:root block is a partial excerpt the final stylesheet combines it with additional custom properties defined later on.).

Recent findings suggest that viewport-based fluid type does not know how wide its element is. A heading in a narrow sidebar can therefore scale as though it fills the viewport.

container-type: inline-size makes the wrapper a container query, so its children can use cqi: a unit based on the container rather than the viewport. Replacing vw in clamp() lets the same heading scale appropriately in an article column or a 300px sidebar without component-specific media queries.

line-height includes space above the cap-height and below the baseline: half-leading. It becomes obvious when text must align tightly with another element. text-box-trim removes it, while text-box-edge measures from capital-letter caps to the alphabetic baseline. This is a metrics-aware alternative to font-specific negative-margin nudges.

It has been revealed that selectors Level 5 proposes :heading, matching h1 to h6 and [role="heading"]. It has not landed in browsers, so keep it behind an @supports selector() check.

Sources indicate that default heading wrapping can leave one short final line. text-wrap: balance distributes text across its lines and works best for blocks of up to about six lines. For paragraphs, text-wrap: pretty avoids a stranded final word without balancing the whole block. Both replace JavaScript orphan fixers. Editable text needs text-wrap: stable, which prevents each new word from reshuffling the paragraph.

It has been revealed that hyphens: auto relies on the browser’s language dictionaries, so the document needs a correct lang attribute (for example ). Without one the browser has no dictionary to use and won’t be able to hyphenate text. Even with the correct lang, the defaults can leave tiny word fragments or several hyphenated lines in a row.

According to recent reports, hyphenate-limit-chars controls the smallest breakable word and fragments; hyphenate-limit-lines prevents a ladder effect. hyphenate-limit-zone makes breaks less frequent, while hyphenate-limit-last protects the final word. Safari needs the prefixed equivalents, so declare both sets together.

Set code, variables, and headings to hyphens: manual: a broken code word can change meaning, and a hyphenated heading usually reads as an error.

Punctuation marks don’t carry the same visual weight as letters, so a quotation mark sitting at the start of a line can look slightly indented against the text below it. hanging-punctuation lets specified punctuation sit fractionally outside the text block’s edge.

Industry observers note that the first value handles opening punctuation, and last handles closing punctuation at the end of a block, while allow-end lets punctuation hang past the right edge rather than force-wrapping. The result is a text block whose edges read as genuinely flush.

Underlines have a related problem. Browsers apply flat, one-size-fits-all thickness and position regardless of the font’s actual weight.

Industry observers note that text-decoration-thickness: from-font reads the thickness the font’s designer intended. text-underline-offset gives descenders room to breathe, and text-decoration-skip-ink: auto interrupts the underline wherever a descender crosses it rather than drawing straight through the letter.

Variable fonts often include an optical size axis, or opsz. It lets a typeface use thinner strokes at large display sizes and thicker, more legible strokes when set small.

font-optical-sizing: auto lets the font make that adjustment based on its actual rendered size. The @supports block covers the older font-variation-settings syntax some browsers still need, while font-variant-ligatures and font-kerning enable the font’s own ligatures and kerning pairs.

In a recent development, light text on a dark background genuinely reads heavier than the same weight on a light background. Where a font ships a GRAD, or grade, axis, the dark mode block dials that perceived weight down without changing glyph shape or width the way an actual weight change would. Fonts without a GRAD axis safely ignore the setting.

Mixing a monospace font into running prose often exposes a mismatched x-height at the same declared font-size. The size-adjust keyword, set once at the @font-face level, scales that font’s rendered output specifically, leaving the actual font-size value untouched.

According to recent reports, numbers in a table need identical widths so they stack into a clean column on the screen. Conversely, numbers in flowing text don’t need the same treatment and should sit naturally alongside the surrounding words.

The tabular-nums and lining-nums keywords give table digits a fixed width and full cap height. oldstyle-nums and proportional-nums let digits sit alongside lowercase letters without sticking up and disrupting the sentence’s texture.

It has been revealed that font-variant-emoji makes the choice between full-colour and monochrome emoji explicit. Without it, the browser or platform gets to choose a fallback, and the result can vary more than you expect. Apply .emoji-color or .emoji-mono to containers where you want to enforce that choice, rather than setting it globally on the body.

Industry observers note that quote style and character order differ by language and region. English nests single quotes inside double quotes, British English reverses that convention, and French uses guillemets with a thin space.

It has been revealed that the quotes property declares the order for each language through :lang(). The native q element then inserts the right pair through open-quote and close-quote. The same markup can render correctly in each locale without hardcoding characters into the content.

Wrapping the rules in :where() keeps them at zero specificity, so a project can override the quote style with one plain class.

Default sub and sup styling is synthesized. The browser just shrinks the text and shifts the baseline, rather than using glyphs actually designed for that position.

font-variant-position switches to the font’s own purpose-built sub and superscript glyphs where they exist, resetting vertical-align, font-size, and line-height so they don’t fight against the real glyph’s intended size and position. Most typefaces only include proper numerals rather than letters, so check the specific font before applying this broadly.

It has been revealed that :where() always resolves to zero specificity, which is useful for a reset. Every rule here is an opinionated default, and wrapping it in :where() lets a project override a property with a plain class.

Sources indicate that :is() solves a different problem: repetition. The heading selector list appears several times in a typographic stylesheet, and grouping it avoids the risk of forgetting a level.

Unlike :where(), :is() carries the specificity of its most specific argument.

Here’s the complete reset, combining the stable layers. Unsupported declarations are ignored by the browser, so the stylesheet can be adopted gradually.

Industry observers note that much of this CSS removes work that used to leak into other parts of a build. text-wrap can take over orphan handling from JavaScript, container query units keep a component’s type scale tied to its own width, and text-box-trim avoids the negative margins once used to compensate for leading. quotes, font-variant-position, and font-optical-sizing hand several smaller details back to the language and the font instead of a collection of one-off fixes.

Industry observers note that browser support will continue to change, especially for text-wrap and text-box-trim. Unsupported declarations are ignored, but that only helps when the unenhanced typography is acceptable in its own right.

Industry observers note that some of these rules are still too new for a baseline reset. A news article, a marketing page, and an editable product interface do not ask the same things of their text; the set that belongs in yours depends on the font, the content, and the browsers you still need to support.

What to Check Before Adding a Tripo Model to a Website

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1495 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial.
  • According to recent reports, A 3D model can look convincing in a still image and still be awkward on a website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sources indicate that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

According to recent reports, A 3D model can look convincing in a still image and still be awkward on a website. The real questions appear when someone rotates it, loads it on a typical connection, or views it on a narrow phone screen. AI generators have made the first draft of a model cheap, which shifts the work toward the part developers and designers already know: budgets, testing and fallbacks.

In a recent development, this article walks through a web-readiness review for an AI-generated model, using an openwork ceramic vessel generated from a single reference image with Tripo as the worked example. The checks apply equally to output from other generators. It includes a small Node.js script that audits a GLB file against a size budget, and the markup for a lightweight viewer with a static fallback. The model shown is one candidate, so it cannot prove browser speed, mobile behavior, hidden geometry or export compatibility. Those are checks to run on your own asset.

Traditional 3D work involves modeling, polygon layout, materials, scale and export. AI generation can shorten the blank-workspace stage. A beginner may discover the category through a search such as AI 3D model generator free, but an initial candidate is useful only if it survives review.

According to recent reports, for this vessel, start with the negative space, meaning the openings between the ribs. A flattering front view can hide a blocked cavity, a thin wall, or two surfaces passing through each other. Generation moves the bottleneck from making a first shape to deciding whether that shape is usable.

In a recent development, image-to-3D tools use a visual reference to create a model candidate, while text-to-3D routes start from a written prompt. Tripo offers both, and other hosted options include Meshy, Rodin by Hyper3D and 3D AI Studio, all of which list GLB among their export formats, while open-source models such as TripoSR and Stable Fast 3D let you run generation yourself. Features, pricing, licensing and output quality differ and change often, so check each vendor’s current documentation. The image route suits this example because the folds, uneven rim and openings already exist in the source.

Whichever tool you use, it can provide a candidate for inspection. It cannot decide whether the source is licensed, whether the unseen rear structure is believable, or whether the exported asset suits a particular viewer. Those judgments belong to the person publishing the page.

According to recent reports, give the object one job. In a portfolio, this vessel might show how its shell and openings relate. That is narrower than calling it printable, manufacturable or dimensionally accurate. Note what must remain recognizable, and provide a still image if the interactive view fails.

Sources indicate that use an image you own or have permission to reuse. Busy backgrounds can distract an image-based workflow, so isolate the object when possible. One photograph also leaves the back and underside unknown. Treat those areas as review risks, not as details confirmed by the source.

After generation, rotate beyond the familiar front. Check the rear, top, underside and sides. Trace each large opening. Look for merged ribs, intersecting surfaces or an unstable base. A wireframe view, when available, can expose crowded geometry. A single front-facing candidate cannot answer these hidden-angle questions, so check them on your own model.

It has been revealed that record the download size, polygon count and texture dimensions. Polygons are the small flat faces that form the shape, and web viewers draw them as triangles. This matters because generator defaults are often tuned for quality, not for the web. In the generation screenshot for this vessel, the viewer reports roughly 1.95 million faces and the settings show 4K texture quality. That is a fine starting point for inspection but a heavy asset for a phone on a mobile connection. Curved ribs may need many triangles, but the count should still fit your page budget.

glTF is the open format most web viewers expect, and GLB is its single-file form that can bundle geometry, textures and materials. The format does not guarantee good performance, so measure the package. The script below reads a GLB with the open-source glTF Transform library, counts triangles, lists texture sizes, and compares them with a budget. The budget values are placeholders; set your own from your target devices.

According to recent reports, run it with node audit.mjs model.glb after installing @gltf-transform/core. It exits with a non-zero status when the asset is over budget, so you can run it in CI. A short test builds two GLBs with known triangle counts, one small and one with 200,000 triangles, and checks that the first passes and the second fails with the right message:.

Sources indicate that when an asset fails, glTF Transform also has a command line. gltf-transform inspect model.glb reports what is inside a file, and gltf-transform optimize input.glb output.glb --compress draco --texture-compress webp applies geometry and texture compression. Compression and mesh simplification can introduce artifacts, especially around thin ribs and openings, so reopen the result and re-check the angles from Gate 3 instead of accepting a smaller file blindly. Also check that your viewer supports the compression you choose.

According to recent reports, load the asset in the intended viewer at desktop and phone widths. Check framing, touch rotation, keyboard access, scrolling and a slower connection. The Google-backed model-viewer web component is one low-code option, and libraries such as three.js give you more control at the cost of more code. The markup below shows the pieces that matter for a first release: a poster image that loads first, lazy loading so the heavy file waits until needed, a text alternative, and visible controls.

The alt text, a poster and touch-action="pan-y" (so a vertical swipe still scrolls the page on a phone) address the common failures. Check the current model-viewer documentation for attribute names and the recommended script include, since they can change between versions. Also consider the WCAG guidance on non-text content: provide a useful description, and offer instructions plus a static image for people who cannot operate the viewer.

A single front-facing candidate is enough to discuss the method, not to certify a finished web asset. Call it a prototype until the exported file passes the checks required by its actual destination.

The same review pattern can be adapted to an architectural ornament, exhibition object, packaging concept or game prop, but each destination adds its own geometry, scale and delivery requirements. A portfolio may accept an inferred rear surface if that limitation is clear. A sales page, printable file or measured product needs stronger references and technical validation.

Industry observers note that the audit script counts triangles, texture sizes and file size only. It does not detect self-intersections, thin walls, flipped normals or licensing problems, and passing it does not make an asset good. The budget numbers are illustrative, and real limits depend on your audience’s devices and connections. Tool features and terms change, so verify them with the vendor before you rely on them, and treat any speed or quality claims on vendor pages as the vendor’s own.

Sources indicate that inspect the angle you would normally crop out. Confirm input rights, measure the download, and test touch, keyboard and a slow connection. Reread the surrounding copy, because claims of fabrication accuracy or production readiness need supporting evidence. For this vessel, “exploratory web model” is an honest label, and more demanding claims require better references and a specialist review.

Recent findings suggest that decide what visitors should learn or do before adding a 3D viewer. A modest prototype with a useful fallback can beat a dramatic asset that loads slowly or hides limitations.

Do I need to code to create a model with an AI generator? No code is required to generate an initial model candidate in Tripo or similar tools. Publishing it interactively is separate work and usually involves a viewer, hosting, responsive testing and enough HTML or JavaScript knowledge to diagnose problems.

When should I use image-to-3D instead of text-to-3D? Use image-to-3D when a rights-cleared visual should guide the form, and text-to-3D when the idea begins as words. Do not treat the two routes as interchangeable evidence.

It has been revealed that is a generated model ready to publish as soon as it exports? No. Inspect the shape from several angles, measure the delivery package, test the intended viewer and prepare a fallback. Higher-stakes uses may also need specialist geometry, scale, material and rights review.

How can a beginner keep web 3D manageable? Give one object one clear job. Set a file-size target, test desktop and phone widths, keep interaction simple, and retain a still image for readers who cannot load or operate the viewer.

#92647. Unlocking Stable On-Policy RL on TPU with Bitwise-Zero Train–Inference Mismatch

Unlocking Stable On-Policy RL on TPU with Bitwise-Zero Train–Inference Mismatch

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (284 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence.
  • Recent findings suggest that in practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths.
  • Our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence. In LLM RL, the model serves as the policy, π(action | previous tokens), and true on-policy learning requires every action in an revision to be generated and evaluated by that exact same policy. While a synchronous loop ensures each rollout batch is scored using the same weights that generated it, a critical numerical requirement remains: the sampler and trainer must evaluate that policy identically.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths. The sampler chooses each action token during incremental decoding and records its behavior logprob. The trainer evaluates the same token in batched forward-backward passes to compute its current logprob and gradients. Under the same weights, these differing execution paths can still assign different logprobs to the same token and context. The training schedule is on-policy, but the numerical execution has introduced a hidden off-policy gap that compounds over multi-turn trajectories.

Our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap. At the same weights, the sampler and trainer assign bitwise-identical logprobs to the same action and token history—bringing state-of-the-art, true on-policy stability to TPU RL training.

It has been revealed that A reduction is a tree of floating-point additions. Floating-point addition is not associative, so changing the tree changes where rounding occurs. The effect is easier to expose in bfloat16, which retains less precision than float32.
